title: A Mechanistic Study of AI-Text Detection Neurons in Frozen BERT: Sparse Probing and Activation Patching on RAID
summary: AI-generated text detectors achieve high accuracy on standard benchmarks, yet the internal representations that drive these predictions remain poorly understood. We study which neurons in a frozen BERT-base-uncased encoder support AI-text detection, using the RAID benchmark across six generators spanning pure-base and instruction-tuned models. We apply the L1-to-L2 sparse-probing protocol of Gurnee et al. (2023) to all 9,216 CLS hidden-state dimensions (12 layers x 768), which we call neurons. The procedure recovers a stable set of under 1% of neurons per generator, consistent across folds and seeds; a probe restricted to that set retains most of the full-feature detection accuracy. Bidirectional activation patching confirms this set's causal relevance: in both directions it flips predictions an order of magnitude more often than size-matched random sets. Mean-ablating the same neurons leaves accuracy largely intact; the signal is therefore redundantly distributed. Cross-generator analysis reveals a bipartite structure: instruction-tuned generators concentrate 30-36% of stable neurons in BERT's final layer while both base generators fall below 14%, consistent with a layer-12 footprint of post-training alignment. Leave-one-family-out evaluation shows the selected neurons retain 86-94% of the full-feature ceiling on unseen generator families, so a detector can operate on a small fixed subspace without re-identifying neurons per generator.

AI.tldr: The paper identifies a very small, stable subset of BERT neurons that is causally important for detecting AI-generated text across multiple generators, and shows this subset generalizes well and is largely redundant in representation.
AI.motivation: Although AI-text detectors perform well, it is unclear which internal model components actually drive their predictions, and whether these components are shared or differ across generators. Understanding this can improve interpretability, robustness, and cross-model generalization of detectors.
AI.method: Using a frozen BERT-base-uncased encoder and the RAID benchmark over six text generators, the authors apply the L1-to-L2 sparse probing protocol to all 9,216 CLS hidden-state dimensions, selecting a small, stable neuron subset per generator whose activations best support AI-text classification. They then validate causal relevance with bidirectional activation patching, assess redundancy via mean ablations, and analyze cross-generator patterns in neuron distribution and generalization, including leave-one-family-out tests.
AI.result: For each generator, under 1% of neurons are consistently selected across folds and seeds, and a probe restricted to them nearly matches full-feature detection accuracy. Activation patching using these neurons flips predictions an order of magnitude more often than random neuron sets of the same size, confirming causal importance. Mean ablations of the same neurons barely reduce accuracy, indicating the signal is redundantly encoded. Cross-generator analysis shows instruction-tuned generators place 30–36% of stable neurons in BERT’s final layer, while base generators use less than 14% there, suggesting a distinct layer-12 alignment footprint. In leave-one-family-out setups, these neurons preserve 86–94% of the full-feature performance on unseen generator families.
AI.conclusion: AI-text detection in a frozen BERT encoder hinges on a small, causally relevant, and redundantly encoded neuron subset that is stable across runs and substantially shared across generator families. Instruction tuning shifts important detection features toward the final layer, and a detector can effectively operate in a compact, fixed neuron subspace without re-learning which neurons to use for each new generator family.

title: Not All Memories Are Equal: Hierarchical Collaborative Memory for Validity-Aware Retrieval in LLM Agents
summary: In team collaboration scenarios, memory is heterogeneous and continually evolving. Team memories capture collective decisions, protocols, and current consensus, while individual memories preserve member-specific observations, execution traces, and intermediate progress. Existing memory-augmented systems typically retrieve from all stored memories as a flat pool, ranking them by semantic relevance, importance, or recency without modeling hierarchical structure or evolving validity. As a result, they often surface semantically relevant but outdated or conflicting memories, especially individual memories that no longer align with current team consensus, instead of prioritizing currently valid memories. This is particularly problematic when collaborative LLM agents answer user questions, since their responses should be grounded in valid memories. We propose HiCoMER, a framework for hierarchical collaborative memory management and validity-aware retrieval in LLM agents. HiCoMER first maintains the validity of team and individual memories and then retrieves memories that remain valid, rather than retrieving directly from all stored memories. It consists of three components: a Hierarchical Memory Conflict Updater, a Validity-Aware Memory Retriever, and a Memory-Grounded Answer Generator. To evaluate HiCoMER, we construct two new datasets for memory-grounded question answering in collaborative settings. Experiments on both datasets show that HiCoMER consistently outperforms strong baselines by reducing outdated retrieval, preserving current team consensus, and improving downstream QA quality.

AI.tldr: HiCoMER is a hierarchical, validity-aware memory framework for multi-agent LLM collaboration that reduces outdated/conflicting retrieval and improves QA.
AI.motivation: In collaborative LLM-agent settings, both team-level and individual-level memories evolve over time. Existing memory-augmented systems treat all memories as a flat pool and rank them mainly by semantic relevance, importance, or recency. This often surfaces semantically relevant but outdated or conflicting information, especially from individual agents that no longer match the team’s current consensus, harming answer correctness. A mechanism is needed to maintain which memories are currently valid and to respect the hierarchy between team and individual memories.
AI.method: The paper proposes HiCoMER, a hierarchical collaborative memory framework that explicitly tracks memory validity and structures retrieval. It separates team memories (decisions, protocols, consensus) from individual memories (observations, execution traces, partial progress). HiCoMER has three components: (1) a Hierarchical Memory Conflict Updater that detects conflicts between new information and existing memories, updates or invalidates outdated memories, and maintains alignment between individual and team memories; (2) a Validity-Aware Memory Retriever that first filters memories by validity and hierarchy, then retrieves only valid, hierarchy-consistent memories instead of searching the whole pool; and (3) a Memory-Grounded Answer Generator that conditions the LLM’s responses on the retrieved valid memories to produce answers that align with current team consensus.
AI.result: The authors build two new datasets specifically for memory-grounded QA in collaborative multi-agent scenarios. Empirical experiments on these datasets show that HiCoMER reduces retrieval of outdated/conflicting memories, better preserves and reflects the current team consensus, and yields higher-quality QA performance compared to strong memory-augmented baselines that lack hierarchical and validity-aware mechanisms.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical, validity-aware memory management is crucial for collaborative LLM-agent systems. By modeling team vs. individual memories, explicitly tracking conflicts and validity, and conditioning retrieval and generation on currently valid memories, HiCoMER significantly improves memory-grounded QA. This suggests that future multi-agent LLM systems should move beyond flat, purely semantic retrieval toward structured, dynamically updated memory frameworks.

title: Auditing and Repairing LLM-as-Judge Failures in a Production Text-to-SQL Pipeline
summary: Production text-to-SQL pipelines often end with an LLM-as-judge whose agreement with human annotators has never actually been measured. When we checked ours, the deployed gpt-4o-mini judge agreed with two-author gold at only Cohen's kappa = 0.04 on a disagreement-enriched set and 0.42 on a uniform-random spot-check, over-flagging 77.1% of the human-FAITHFUL cases in the enriched set. Most of its over-flags trace back to a single mechanism we call GRADE-HALLUCINATION. A self-hosted Qwen3.6-27B replacement (kappa = 0.72) lands in the same range as Claude Opus 4.7 (kappa = 0.71); the head-to-head is underpowered at n = 96, but for the deployment decision that hardly matters, since Qwen costs roughly 1/300 as much per call. Ensembling does not help for free. Pairing the weak judge with a stronger one degrades agreement, whereas three strong judges under unanimity routing reach kappa = 0.79 at 89.7% auto-coverage. Applied out-of-domain, the same audit recipe flags 25.5% of BIRD-financial's expert-authored gold SQLs as candidate gold-SQL issues under our annotation protocol. Code and pre-registration are at https://github.com/JamesL404/synca-audit.

AI.tldr: The paper audits LLM-as-judge components in text-to-SQL pipelines, finds a widely deployed small judge is very unreliable, identifies a specific hallucination pattern, and shows that a cheap, stronger local model or a careful ensemble of strong judges can greatly improve reliability and coverage while also revealing issues in existing gold SQL datasets.
AI.motivation: Many production text-to-SQL systems use an LLM-as-judge to automatically assess whether generated SQL is faithful to the user’s request. However, the reliability of these automatic judges is usually assumed rather than empirically verified. This paper is motivated by the need to rigorously measure how well such judges agree with human annotators, to understand failure modes such as systematic hallucinations, to compare cheaper local models with expensive frontier models, and to evaluate whether ensembling judges actually improves quality. It also aims to test whether the same auditing methodology can surface problems in benchmark gold SQL labels themselves.
AI.method: The authors audit a deployed text-to-SQL pipeline where an LLM serves as an automatic judge of faithfulness. They measure agreement between the LLM judge (gpt-4o-mini) and a two-author human gold standard using Cohen’s kappa, on both a disagreement-enriched evaluation set and a uniform-random spot-check sample. They analyze over-flagged cases to identify a dominant failure mechanism termed GRADE-HALLUCINATION. They then evaluate an alternative, self-hosted Qwen3.6-27B judge and compare its kappa with that of Claude Opus 4.7. To study ensembling, they experiment with combinations of weak and strong judges under unanimity-based routing and report resulting kappa and automatic coverage. Finally, they apply the same audit protocol to the BIRD-financial dataset to see how often expert-authored gold SQLs are flagged as problematic under their annotation scheme. All code and a pre-registration are released for reproducibility.
AI.result: The original deployed judge, gpt-4o-mini, shows very low agreement with the two-author human gold: Cohen’s kappa is 0.04 on a disagreement-enriched set and 0.42 on a random spot-check. It over-flags 77.1% of cases that humans label as FAITHFUL, with most errors attributable to a single failure mode (GRADE-HALLUCINATION). By contrast, a self-hosted Qwen3.6-27B judge achieves kappa = 0.72, comparable to Claude Opus 4.7 (kappa = 0.71), while costing about 1/300 as much per call. Ensembling is not uniformly beneficial: combining a weak and strong judge actually reduces agreement, whereas an ensemble of three strong judges using unanimity routing attains kappa = 0.79 with 89.7% automatic coverage. Applying the audit approach to the BIRD-financial dataset, 25.5% of expert-authored gold SQL queries are flagged as potential issues according to their protocol.
AI.conclusion: LLM-as-judge components in text-to-SQL pipelines can be far less reliable than assumed, with small, inexpensive frontier models like gpt-4o-mini substantially over-flagging faithful outputs and exhibiting systematic hallucination behaviors. Careful empirical auditing is therefore essential. The study shows that strong, self-hosted open models such as Qwen3.6-27B can match the reliability of expensive proprietary models at a fraction of the cost, making them attractive deployment options. Naive ensembling, especially mixing weak and strong judges, can hurt reliability, but ensembles of multiple strong judges with strict unanimity criteria can further boost agreement while retaining high coverage. The same audit methodology is also powerful enough to uncover potential problems in supposedly expert-curated gold SQL datasets, indicating that benchmark quality itself should be questioned. Overall, the paper argues for systematic audits, stronger local judges, and carefully designed ensembles rather than blind trust in a single LLM judge.

title: A Survey on Fake Review Detection: From Pre-trained Language Models to Large Language Models
comment: Fanji Yang and Huiyao Chen contributed equally to this work. Accepted for publication in Information Fusion
summary: Online reviews shape consumer decisions, platform governance, and corporate reputation.Fake reviews compromise this information channel by injecting deceptive evidence into rating systems, recommendation pipelines, and public trust mechanisms.The rise of large language models, or LLMs, has changed the problem in two directions.LLMs can generate fluent and context-aware deceptive reviews, while pre-trained language models, or PLMs, and LLMs also provide stronger semantic representations for detection.This survey reviews fake review detection from an information fusion perspective, covering 211 studies published from 2018 to early 2026.We organize existing work by evidence source and fusion level, covering review text, sentiment, rating behavior, temporal metadata, user-product graphs, multimodal content, external knowledge, and LLM-generated signals.We trace the development from traditional machine learning and deep learning to PLM-based and LLM-based methods, and examine how different approaches combine textual, behavioral, structural, and multimodal evidence.We also analyze reported performance trends on widely used Amazon, Yelp, and OpSpam benchmark families, while noting the limitations caused by different label construction procedures, data splits, and evaluation protocols.Finally, we identify open problems in adversarial generation, cross-domain transfer, uncertainty-aware fusion, missing-source robustness, interpretability, and trustworthy evaluation for AI-generated deceptive content.

AI.tldr: Survey of fake online review detection methods from an information-fusion viewpoint, focusing on how diverse signals and modern language models are combined, what works on major benchmarks, and what open challenges remain in the LLM era.
AI.motivation: Fake online reviews increasingly distort consumer decisions, platform governance, and reputations, especially as large language models make generating realistic deceptive text easier. At the same time, modern pre-trained and large language models provide powerful semantic representations for detecting such fraud. However, research is fragmented across different signals (text, behavior, graphs, multimodal, etc.) and model paradigms, making it hard to see how evidence is fused and where gaps remain. A systematic survey is needed to unify these strands, clarify progress on standard benchmarks, and highlight limitations and open problems in the age of AI-generated deception.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured survey of 211 papers on fake review detection published between 2018 and early 2026. They categorize work by the types of evidence used (review text, sentiment, rating patterns, temporal data, user–item graphs, multimodal signals, external knowledge, and LLM-based signals) and by the fusion level (feature-level, model-level, decision-level, etc.). They trace the chronological evolution from traditional ML and deep learning to pre-trained language model-based and LLM-based approaches, and they synthesize reported experimental results on widely adopted benchmark datasets such as Amazon, Yelp, and OpSpam, while critically examining differences in labeling, splitting, and evaluation protocols.
AI.result: The survey finds a clear progression from shallow, single-source methods to richer, multi-source fusion approaches that integrate textual, behavioral, structural, and multimodal cues, increasingly powered by PLMs and LLMs. Reported performance generally improves over time on common benchmarks, particularly when strong text encoders and multi-evidence fusion are used. However, the results are not always directly comparable due to heterogeneous dataset constructions, label generation strategies, train–test splits, and evaluation setups, which can obscure the true gains and robustness of proposed methods.
AI.conclusion: Fake review detection has benefited substantially from advances in PLMs and LLMs and from more systematic fusion of heterogeneous signals, but the field still faces major challenges. Key open problems include dealing with adversarially generated reviews, enabling robust cross-domain transfer, designing uncertainty-aware and missing-source-resilient fusion methods, improving interpretability of detection decisions, and developing more reliable, standardized, and trustworthy evaluation protocols tailored to AI-generated deceptive content.

title: Cartograph: Federated Tool Discovery with Operator-Attested Retrieval for AI Agents
summary: The Model Context Protocol (MCP) enables AI agents to discover and call tools, but loading every definition becomes expensive as connected catalogs grow. We present Cartograph, a federated MCP proxy that changes agent-visible tool discovery from $O(n)$ catalog traversal to $O(k)$ progressive disclosure. Cartograph combines three mechanisms: (1) operator-attested capability cards, Ed25519-signed descriptions generated under the deploying operator's control rather than ranked publisher copy; (2) Rift, a three-layer confusable-cluster analysis comprising density clustering, query-margin analysis, and token diagnosis; and (3) two-stage retrieval, which ranks servers before tools. On a 22-server, 374-tool deployment, Cartograph exposes three proxy tools instead of 374 definitions. A 49-query author-constructed benchmark yields R@5 of 0.816, compared with 0.592 for a Jaccard keyword baseline, while a measured top-5 discovery exchange uses 475 tokens rather than 42,450 under the stated full-catalog accounting. Rift identifies 49 confusable clusters, including four HIGH-risk clusters in bootstrap-generated cards. An exploratory comparison of 119 LLM-generated descriptions removes the observed zero-distance cluster but shows that mixing card-generation regimes can reduce R@5. Gateway measurements over ten trials add 5ms mean latency (0.8%) relative to direct stdio MCP calls. Cartograph is complementary to code-execution approaches: it controls which tool descriptions are surfaced and records the provenance of the descriptions used for ranking for each query.

AI.tldr: Cartograph is a federated MCP proxy that makes tool discovery more efficient and safer by progressively disclosing tools instead of loading all tool definitions at once.
AI.motivation: As MCP-connected catalogs grow, having agents load and traverse every tool definition becomes computationally expensive and unwieldy, and naive keyword-based discovery performs poorly and can create confusable or risky tool groupings.
AI.method: The authors design Cartograph, a proxy for MCP, with three main mechanisms: (1) operator-attested, Ed25519-signed capability cards describing tools under operator control; (2) Rift, a three-layer confusable-cluster analysis pipeline (density clustering, query-margin analysis, token diagnosis) to detect and manage similar or risky tools; and (3) a two-stage retrieval process that first ranks servers, then their tools, enabling progressive disclosure of only the most relevant tools to the agent.
AI.result: In a deployment with 22 servers and 374 tools, Cartograph exposes just three proxy tools instead of 374 full definitions. On a 49-query benchmark it achieves R@5 of 0.816 vs 0.592 for a Jaccard keyword baseline, and reduces tokens for a top-5 discovery exchange from 42,450 to 475. Rift finds 49 confusable clusters (four HIGH-risk). Using 119 LLM-generated descriptions removes one pathological zero-distance cluster but mixing human and LLM descriptions can reduce retrieval quality. Added gateway latency is only about 5ms (0.8%) compared to direct MCP calls.
AI.conclusion: Cartograph efficiently scales MCP tool discovery, significantly reducing token and catalog overhead while improving retrieval quality with minimal latency. Its confusability analysis surfaces safety and overlap issues, and its design complements code-execution approaches by deciding which tool descriptions are shown and by tracking provenance of descriptions used in ranking.

title: SlideLab: Audience-Centered Scientific Slide Generation and Evaluation
summary: Scientific presentations are more than summaries of research papers. They need to present the work in a coherent sequence, explain the main ideas clearly, and help the audience follow the presentation. We present SlideLab, a training-free multi-agent framework for generating scientific presentations from research papers. SlideLab first plans the presentation narrative, then builds and iteratively refines a shared slide deck using agents for content planning, visual generation, layout refinement, and grounding verification. In a blind human preference study, SlideLab was preferred over both open-source and commercial systems on 77% of papers while using roughly 4 times fewer inference tokens than the strongest open-source baseline. We also introduce ConfArena, an audience-oriented evaluation framework that simulates a conference room and assesses presentations slide by slide. ConfArena matches human system rankings and detects injected presentation problems, including falsified numbers, degraded figures, dropped slides, and shuffled slide order.

AI.tldr: Introduces SlideLab, a multi-agent system that automatically generates coherent scientific slide decks from papers, plus ConfArena, a framework to evaluate such presentations.
AI.motivation: Existing systems often treat slide generation as a direct summarization problem, producing slides that are poorly structured, unclear, and hard to follow. There is also a lack of robust, scalable evaluation methods that reflect how audiences actually experience scientific talks. The authors aim to create a method that can generate more coherent, audience-friendly presentations and a realistic evaluation framework that can detect quality issues and misalignments between slides and the underlying paper.
AI.method: They design SlideLab, a training-free multi-agent framework where specialized agents collaborate to produce and refine a slide deck from a research paper. The process first plans the narrative, then builds and iteratively improves slides through content-planning, visual-generation, layout-refinement, and grounding-verification agents, all sharing a common slide representation. For evaluation, they conduct a blind human preference study comparing SlideLab to open-source and commercial baselines. They also propose ConfArena, an audience-oriented evaluation framework that simulates a conference setting and scores talks slide by slide, including tests where specific presentation errors are injected to see if the framework detects them.
AI.result: In human blind evaluations, SlideLab is preferred in 77% of cases over both open-source and commercial slide-generation systems while using about four times fewer inference tokens than the strongest open-source baseline, indicating both higher quality and better efficiency. ConfArena’s system rankings align with human judgments and it successfully identifies injected issues such as falsified numbers, degraded figures, omitted slides, and shuffled slide orders.
AI.conclusion: A training-free multi-agent approach can substantially improve automated generation of scientific presentations in terms of coherence, clarity, and audience alignment while being more token-efficient. Furthermore, an audience-centric evaluation environment like ConfArena can reliably approximate human assessments and detect subtle presentation defects, offering a practical way to benchmark and stress-test presentation-generation systems.

title: SignTrace: Describe a Sign, Find the Word
comment: Includes reproducibility data and method documentation
summary: Identifying an unfamiliar sign is difficult when a learner remembers its movement but does not know its meaning or formal feature codes. SignTrace addresses this longstanding reverse-lookup problem through natural-language access to a Chinese sign-language dictionary. The system integrates LLM-based dictionary enrichment, action extraction, dictionary-style rewriting, seven-channel retrieval, and candidate reranking over 6,699 entries. It has been deployed for user trials and has received positive informal feedback. Evaluation on a dictionary-derived benchmark of 500 movement-description queries yields 94.0% Hit@1, 97.4% Hit@9, and a mean reciprocal rank of 0.9540. Reranking increases Hit@1 from 71.8% to 94.0%, while component analyses show the contribution of enriched entry descriptions. Median query-processing time is 13.37 seconds with six concurrent queries. By connecting everyday movement descriptions to documented signs and meanings, SignTrace provides a practical tool for identifying unfamiliar signs. Dictionary-derived wording and prior selection within the benchmark limit generalization to descriptions independently produced by users.

AI.tldr: A system called SignTrace enables reverse lookup of Chinese sign language signs from natural-language movement descriptions, achieving high retrieval accuracy through LLM-based dictionary enrichment, multi-channel retrieval, and reranking.
AI.motivation: Learners often remember how a sign moves but not its meaning or formal notation, making it hard to identify signs in existing dictionaries that rely on knowing formal feature codes or glosses. There is a need for a practical tool that supports natural-language, movement-based lookup for sign language learners.
AI.method: The authors build SignTrace, which enriches dictionary entries for 6,699 Chinese Sign Language signs using LLMs, extracts action information, rewrites entries in dictionary style, and indexes them across seven retrieval channels. At query time, users input natural-language movement descriptions; the system retrieves candidate signs across channels and applies a reranking step to improve accuracy. They evaluate using a benchmark of 500 movement-description queries derived from the dictionary itself and analyze the impact of individual system components.
AI.result: On the 500-query benchmark, SignTrace attains 94.0% Hit@1, 97.4% Hit@9, and an MRR of 0.9540. The reranking module improves Hit@1 from 71.8% to 94.0%, and ablation/component analyses reveal that enriching entry descriptions significantly contributes to performance. The system has been deployed for user trials and has obtained positive informal user feedback. Median latency is 13.37 seconds with six queries processed concurrently.
AI.conclusion: SignTrace effectively solves the reverse-lookup problem for Chinese Sign Language from natural-language motion descriptions, offering a practical sign-identification tool with strong retrieval performance. However, because the evaluation benchmark is derived from dictionary wording and preselected signs, its generalizability to free-form user descriptions is limited, indicating a need for further testing on independently produced queries.

title: Bootstrapping Conversational Recommendation Agents At Spotify: Synthetic Data Generation and Self-Improvement Loops
summary: Conversational recommendation agents are a new paradigm for content discovery, enabling users to express complex intents through natural language (e.g., "recommend Italian indie artists I haven't heard before"). A central challenge in building such agents is optimizing agent planning -- deciding how to select, sequence, and invoke tools -- particularly in cold-start settings where real user interactions are not yet available. We introduce a pipeline for multi-turn synthetic data generation and a self-improvement loop to address this challenge. The synthetic data pipeline transforms single-turn prompts into realistic multi-turn conversations, enabling systematic evaluation before launch. The self-improvement loop combines variance-based contrastive optimization with iterative refinement through a coding agent, automatically identifying and fixing planning and tool-use errors. Our approach improves quality by +8% on top of a highly optimized manual prompt. The system has been productionized and significantly accelerated iteration cycles for the launch of a conversational recommendation agent at Spotify. Online A/B tests demonstrate its effectiveness, with +14% user listening, +5% increase in weekly active users, and a 5% reduction in skip rate compared to a prior experience supporting only session refinement. This work provides a practical framework for accelerating the development of conversational recommendation agents in industry.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a practical framework that uses synthetic multi-turn conversations and a self-improvement loop to optimize tool-planning for conversational recommendation agents before real user data is available, leading to measurable gains in production at Spotify.
AI.motivation: Building effective conversational recommendation agents is hard because the agent must plan how to select, sequence, and use tools over multiple turns, especially in cold-start scenarios where there is little or no real interaction data to guide optimization. Manual prompt engineering and ad hoc testing are slow and do not systematically reveal planning failures, which slows down iteration and deployment in industrial settings.
AI.method: The authors propose (1) a pipeline that converts single-turn prompts into realistic multi-turn synthetic conversations, allowing controlled offline evaluation of different agent-planning strategies; and (2) a self-improvement loop that performs variance-based contrastive optimization over these synthetic dialogues, combined with an automatic coding agent that iteratively inspects failures in planning/tool use and edits the agent’s prompts or tool logic to fix them. This loop repeatedly generates data, evaluates behavior, identifies errors, and applies code/prompt updates without human-in-the-loop for each iteration.
AI.result: Using this framework on a conversational recommendation agent at Spotify, the authors report an 8% quality improvement relative to an already highly tuned manual prompt in offline evaluation. When deployed to production and tested via online A/B experiments, the improved agent led to 14% higher user listening, a 5% increase in weekly active users, and a 5% reduction in content skip rate compared with a previous experience that only supported session refinement rather than full conversational recommendation.
AI.conclusion: A structured synthetic data pipeline combined with an automated self-improvement loop can significantly accelerate the design and optimization of conversational recommendation agents. By enabling robust pre-launch evaluation and continuous automated refinement of planning and tool use, this framework delivers measurable business and user-engagement gains in an industrial setting and offers a generalizable approach for developing similar agents in other domains.

title: A Unified Account of Concepts and Chunks
summary: Cognitive psychology has studied how people encode, use, and learn concepts that describe categories, and how they represent, recognize, and acquire chunks for familiar patterns of elements. The literatures on these two topics are nearly disjoint, which poses a challenge for unified theories of cognition. In this paper, we review Cobweb, a computational account of categorization and concept formation, and propose an extended theory that incorporates chunks and their acquisition. The theory makes no commitments about modality, applying to any experience that decomposes into elements and relations among them. We also present \trellis/, an implementation of this theory, and illustrate its application to learning context-free grammars, which we adopt as a testbed because they involve both concept-like and chunk-like elements. In addition, we report experimental results on three synthetic grammars that demonstrate the system's ability to represent syntactic knowledge, use it to parse and generate sentences, and learn compositional structures from sample parses. We conclude by discussing related work on concepts and chunks, along with directions for future research in the area.

AI.tldr: The paper unifies concept categorization and chunk acquisition via an extended Cobweb theory, implemented in the TRELLIS system, and validates it on learning context-free grammars.
AI.motivation: Research on human concepts (categories) and chunks (familiar patterns) has evolved in largely separate literatures, which is problematic for building unified theories of cognition. The authors want a single, modality-independent account that explains how both conceptual categories and chunks are represented, learned, and used, and that can be tested computationally on structured domains like grammars.
AI.method: They start from Cobweb, a computational model of categorization and concept formation, and extend it to also handle chunks and their acquisition in a modality-general way. They implement this extended theory in a system called TRELLIS and use context-free grammars as a testbed. Through experiments on three synthetic grammars, they evaluate how well TRELLIS can learn, represent, and use syntactic knowledge. The evaluation includes tasks such as parsing, sentence generation, and learning compositional structures from sample parses.
AI.result: TRELLIS successfully acquires representations of syntactic knowledge from examples of parses of sentences generated by three different synthetic context-free grammars. It can use these learned structures to parse new sentences, generate sentences, and capture compositional relations that reflect both concept-like and chunk-like elements in the grammar. This shows that the extended theory can handle both kinds of cognitive structures within one framework.
AI.conclusion: The authors conclude that their extension of Cobweb, instantiated in TRELLIS, offers a plausible unified account of concepts and chunks that is modality-independent and effective on structured domains such as context-free grammars. They argue that this bridges a gap between two previously separate literatures, and they situate their work within related research on concepts and chunks while outlining future directions for developing more comprehensive theories of cognition and for applying their framework to other domains.

title: CARGO: Context-Aware Retrieval-Gated Evaluation of Agentic AI in Production
summary: Reference-based LLM-as-a-judge evaluation assumes the reference answer is the target. In deployed agentic systems that operate over dynamic entities (support cases, assets, accounts), the closest available reference typically applies the correct procedure to a different entity, so a literal judge penalizes different identifiers, dates, and statuses as errors or hallucinations. We name this failure mode reference-instance divergence (RID). We propose CARGO, a framework that (i) treats retrieved references as procedural exemplars and grounds factual judgments in the live instance's observed context, (ii) assigns each claim a three-way status (supported, contradicted, unverifiable) and penalizes only contradictions, and (iii) gates evaluation by retrieval confidence, casting production evaluation as selective prediction. We introduce CARGO-Bench, a perturbation-based diagnostic suite with ground truth by construction that separates leniency from discrimination. On CARGO-Bench (246 items, two judge models, 7,872 judgments), the standard reference-based judge penalizes 100% of correct entity-transplanted answers and is uninformative (discrimination index DI ~ 0); supplying the live facts without reframing changes nothing. CARGO eliminates these false penalties (0/50) while retaining near-complete contradiction recall (50/50 and 49/50), raising DI to 0.58 [0.48, 0.68]; a rubric-swap control attributes most of the effect to context-grounded dimension definitions. CARGO also exposes a limitation of its own design: the leniency that protects entity values suppresses detection of procedural corruptions (20% recall). A post-hoc fix does not close the gap, and an LLM-as-annotator study with written guidelines and adjudication shows the same blind spot. We release a preregistered protocol for extending the evaluation to expert agreement, risk-coverage, and cost on production traffic.

AI.tldr: CARGO is a framework for evaluating LLM-generated answers in dynamic, entity-specific settings by treating references as procedural templates, grounding judgments in live context, and penalizing only factual contradictions.
AI.motivation: Standard reference-based LLM-as-a-judge evaluations wrongly assume that the reference answer’s entity (e.g., a particular account or ticket) is the same as the live entity, which causes correct, entity-specific variations to be misjudged as hallucinations or errors—a problem the authors term reference-instance divergence (RID). This makes current evaluation methods unreliable for deployed, agentic systems over dynamic entities.
AI.method: The authors propose CARGO, which: (i) treats retrieved references as procedural exemplars while grounding factual judgments in the current instance’s observed context, (ii) labels each claim as supported, contradicted, or unverifiable and penalizes only contradictions, and (iii) gates evaluation by retrieval confidence, framing production evaluation as selective prediction. They also create CARGO-Bench, a perturbation-based diagnostic benchmark with constructed ground truth, and run extensive experiments (246 items, 2 judge models, 7,872 judgments) including rubric-swap controls and an LLM-as-annotator study with guidelines and adjudication.
AI.result: On CARGO-Bench, standard reference-based judges penalize 100% of correct entity-transplanted answers and have almost no discriminative power (DI ≈ 0), and even providing live facts without reframing does not help. CARGO removes these false penalties (0/50) while preserving nearly all contradiction detection (50/50 and 49/50), boosting the discrimination index to 0.58 [0.48, 0.68]. A rubric-swap control indicates that context-grounded dimension definitions drive most of this improvement. However, CARGO shows low recall (20%) for detecting procedural corruptions; a post-hoc fix and an LLM-as-annotator study reveal this as a fundamental blind spot.
AI.conclusion: CARGO is an effective framework for evaluating LLM outputs in dynamic, entity-specific environments by focusing on contradictions relative to live context rather than literal agreement with a static reference. It substantially improves discrimination between correct and incorrect answers in the presence of reference-instance divergence but is less sensitive to procedural errors. The authors provide a preregistered protocol to extend evaluation toward expert agreement, risk-coverage, and cost on real production traffic.

title: Breaking Homogeneity: Diversifying Persona Sets for Creative LLM Outputs
summary: Language models often produce homogeneous responses to open-ended tasks; such homogeneity can spawn groupthink-the convergence of ideas toward a singular and potentially suboptimal decision. We formulate persona diversification as a set-level conditioning problem and study two orthogonal design choices: selecting versus generating personas, and space-filling versus frontier-seeking diversity. We instantiate this design space with four methods spanning coverage and dispersion subset selections, uniform-coverage sampling, and evolutionary persona generation. Evaluations on the Alternative Uses Task (AUT), Infinity-Chat, and Divergent Association Task (DAT) show the benefits of the proposed methods across tasks and creativity objectives. On AUT, evolutionary persona generation increases response diversity by 78.8%, originality by 26.1%, flexibility by 49.5%, and holistic creativity by 13.9% over task-only prompting, while maintaining 98.5% validity; on Infinity-Chat, it nearly doubles persona-induced response separation relative to random personas. Moreover, evolutionary personas compose with creativity-optimized prompting, further increasing its response diversity by 18.6% and creativity by 6.3%. These results establish persona-set geometry as a task-agnostic mechanism for eliciting divergent LLM outputs, and support persona diversification as a reusable complement to prompt optimization.

AI.tldr: The paper tackles the problem of groupthink and homogeneous outputs in language models by diversifying 'personas' used to condition generation, showing this increases creativity and diversity of responses across several tasks.
AI.motivation: Language models tend to output similar, convergent answers to open-ended and creative tasks, which can lead to groupthink and limit their usefulness for ideation, brainstorming, and creativity support. The authors want a general, task-agnostic way to systematically elicit diverse, divergent outputs from LLMs rather than just tuning a single prompt.
AI.method: They formulate 'persona diversification' as a set-level conditioning problem: instead of a single persona or generic prompt, they construct a set of personas whose geometry in embedding/feature space is controlled. They explore two axes of design: (1) whether personas are selected from a pool or generated, and (2) whether the diversity objective is space-filling (broad coverage) or frontier-seeking (pushing to extremes). They instantiate four concrete methods: coverage-based subset selection, dispersion-based subset selection, uniform-coverage sampling, and evolutionary persona generation that iteratively mutates/selects personas to maximize diversity and creativity-related objectives. They then plug these persona sets into LLM prompting pipelines and evaluate across tasks.
AI.result: Across three benchmarks (Alternative Uses Task, Infinity-Chat, Divergent Association Task), their persona diversification methods consistently increase response diversity and creativity-relevant metrics compared to standard task-only prompting and random personas. On AUT, evolutionary persona generation yields large relative gains: +78.8% response diversity, +26.1% originality, +49.5% flexibility, +13.9% holistic creativity, with 98.5% validity, and on Infinity-Chat it nearly doubles the separation of responses attributable to personas vs random personas. Combining evolutionary personas with creativity-optimized prompting further boosts diversity by 18.6% and creativity by 6.3%.
AI.conclusion: Designing and controlling the geometry of sets of personas is an effective, task-agnostic lever for eliciting divergent, creative outputs from LLMs and mitigating groupthink. Persona diversification works as a reusable complement to standard prompt optimization and can be composed with other creativity-enhancing techniques, suggesting a general strategy for improving LLM-based ideation systems.

title: The Price of Thought: Does Test-Time Reasoning Pay in LLM Trading?
summary: While inference-time reasoning in large language models (LLMs) promises better decision making, its higher computational cost may not yield better economic outcomes. Yet reasoning controls are rarely evaluated as economic interventions, where changes in model outputs must translate into better portfolios after trading costs. We conduct a controlled study of representative LLMs from the DeepSeek, GPT, and Gemini families. We vary reasoning effort while holding information available at each formation date, prompts, output formats, and portfolio construction fixed. Our evaluation covers a full year of U.S. equities under three input conditions: numerical, identifiable news, and masked news. It includes more than 800,000 asset predictions and repeated model generations. Across all three model families, additional reasoning does not produce a reliable improvement in net portfolio returns. For DeepSeek, where we examine the full progression from no reasoning to maximum reasoning, performance is nonmonotonic. Repeated generations also produce unstable treatment effects and portfolio selections, even when overall scores remain similar. These findings show that additional reasoning can change financial decisions without reliably improving their economic value, motivating validation for each task before deployment.

AI.tldr: The paper empirically tests whether increasing inference-time reasoning in LLMs improves real trading performance, finding that more reasoning generally fails to yield more profitable portfolios after costs.
AI.motivation: Reasoning modes in LLMs (e.g., chain-of-thought, more steps, repeated sampling) are often assumed to improve decision quality, but are rarely evaluated in terms of actual economic outcomes where trading costs and portfolio performance matter. The authors aim to understand whether extra computational effort for reasoning is economically justified in quantitative equity investing.
AI.method: The authors run a controlled experiment on U.S. equities over one year, using several representative LLM families (DeepSeek, GPT, Gemini). They fix inputs (information set per date), prompts, output schema, and portfolio construction method, and systematically vary only the level of inference-time reasoning. They consider three input types (pure numerical data, explicit/identifiable news, and news where key identifiers are masked). They generate more than 800,000 asset-level predictions, including repeated generations, then translate these predictions into portfolios and evaluate net returns after trading costs, while analyzing how reasoning depth and repeated sampling affect performance and portfolio stability.
AI.result: Across the three model families, increasing reasoning effort does not consistently improve net portfolio returns; in many cases, it yields no benefit or even worse performance. For DeepSeek, examining the full spectrum from no reasoning to maximum reasoning reveals a nonmonotonic relationship between reasoning depth and returns. Repeated generations induce unstable treatment effects and frequent changes in portfolio holdings, despite similar average prediction scores, indicating that decision-level outcomes are sensitive and noisy even when surface metrics look stable.
AI.conclusion: Inference-time reasoning controls in LLMs can substantially alter financial decisions without reliably improving their economic value. Extra computational cost for more reasoning is not automatically justified in trading applications. Therefore, reasoning settings should be validated for each specific financial task and environment before deployment, rather than assumed beneficial by default.

title: Inquesto Score: A reliability Protocol For Voice Agents
summary: Voice agents are increasingly deployed in workflows where failed interactions can affect transactions, access, and other consequential outcomes, creating a need for reproducible and interpretable evaluation. We introduce Inquesto Score (IS), a protocol for measuring voice-agent reliability as the percentage of calls in a fixed, versioned evaluation population that achieve the caller's goal without a functional failure or worse. Rather than combining heterogeneous metrics, IS defines explicit failure events and severity levels and evaluates the deployed voice pipeline. Timing failures, including talk-over and delayed responses, are measured directly from audio, while semantic and state-dependent failures are evaluated using scenario predicates, tool traces, and a pinned open-model judge. Diagnostic views of behavior, acoustic robustness, identity handling, and speaker groups accompany the score without being combined into it. Inquesto Score v0.1 evaluates 30 scenarios, three acoustic conditions, four speaker groups, and 306 calls per agent across 13 configurations of a reference voice-agent system. Our evaluation shows that reliable measurement requires evidence beyond transcripts, explicit treatment of deployment conditions, and validation of the evaluators used to determine outcomes. We release the protocol, reference implementation, and evaluation records.

AI.tldr: Introduces Inquesto Score, a standardized, interpretable reliability metric for voice agents based on functional success/failure in controlled evaluation scenarios.
AI.motivation: Voice agents are now used in high-stakes workflows (transactions, access control, etc.), where failures have real consequences. Existing evaluations often combine heterogeneous metrics (e.g., ASR accuracy, task success, latency) in ad-hoc ways, rely only on transcripts, and are not fully reproducible or interpretable at the system level. There is a need for a principled, versioned evaluation protocol that reflects real deployment conditions and produces a single reliability score that is grounded in explicit failure definitions.
AI.method: Define Inquesto Score (IS) as the percentage of calls in a fixed, versioned evaluation population that successfully achieve the caller’s goal without incurring a failure of a specified severity or worse. Failures are explicitly categorized (including timing failures like talk-over and delays, semantic and state-dependent errors). The protocol evaluates the full deployed voice pipeline. Timing failures are measured directly from audio signals; semantic and state-dependent failures are detected using scenario-specific predicates, tool traces, and a pinned open-model judge. IS is accompanied by diagnostic views (behavior, acoustic robustness, identity handling, speaker groups) that are reported but not aggregated into the main score. The authors implement IS v0.1 with 30 scenarios, three acoustic conditions, four speaker groups, and 306 calls per agent, and test 13 configurations of a reference voice-agent system.
AI.result: Inquesto Score v0.1 is able to systematically evaluate voice agents across multiple scenarios, acoustic conditions, speaker groups, and system configurations. The experiments show that relying only on transcripts is insufficient for accurate reliability measurement; evaluation must incorporate audio-based timing evidence, explicit modeling of deployment conditions, and careful validation of evaluators (including model judges and scenario predicates). The protocol and tooling successfully generate a single reliability score plus rich diagnostics, demonstrating its practical feasibility.
AI.conclusion: Inquesto Score provides a reproducible, interpretable, and deployment-grounded protocol for measuring voice-agent reliability. By defining explicit failure events and severities, leveraging audio and system traces, and separating the main score from diagnostic breakdowns, it addresses limitations of prior ad-hoc or transcript-only evaluations. The released protocol, reference implementation, and records enable standardized benchmarking and more trustworthy assessment of voice agents used in consequential workflows.

title: Probing Stability-Plasticity Tradeoffs in Agent Memory through Cognitive Experimental Paradigms
comment: Accepted by EMNLP 2026 Main, code is availble at https://github.com/jq-ding/MemProbe
summary: Agent memory systems are increasingly used to maintain long-term user preferences, task states and evolving facts, but current evaluations often collapse memory behavior into final-answer accuracy. We introduce MemProbe, a cognitive-science-inspired framework for diagnosing stability-plasticity tradeoffs in agent memory. The framework is motivated by a core insight from cognitive memory research: memory is reconstructive and shaped by interference, source reliability, reinforcement, and reactivation. MemProbe turns this insight into four reusable experimental paradigms (interference, misinformation, consolidation strength, and reconsolidation window) that manipulate when a memory should be updated, preserved, or treated as uncertain. It further decomposes correctness into behavioral profiles that reveal how systems update, preserve, attribute, and temporally organize information. We instantiate these paradigms in a 56-episode diagnostic suite and evaluate six incremental memory systems under a unified protocol. Results show that systems with similar aggregate scores exhibit distinct behavioral profiles. MemProbe provides such a diagnostic lens, turning aggregate performance into interpretable profiles of memory maintenance over time. Code is available at https://github.com/jq-ding/MemProbe.

AI.tldr: MemProbe is a diagnostic framework to analyze how agent memory systems balance stability and plasticity, going beyond final-answer accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of agent memory systems reduce memory behavior to final-answer accuracy, which hides how systems actually update, preserve, and organize long-term information. Cognitive science shows memory is reconstructive and influenced by interference, source reliability, reinforcement, and reactivation, suggesting richer ways to probe memory behavior.
AI.method: The authors design MemProbe, a set of four experimental paradigms—interference, misinformation, consolidation strength, and reconsolidation window—that manipulate when an agent should update, preserve, or be uncertain about memories. They decompose evaluation into behavioral profiles capturing updating, preservation, attribution, and temporal organization. They implement these paradigms in a 56-episode diagnostic suite and test six incremental memory systems under a unified protocol.
AI.result: Across the six evaluated memory systems, models with similar overall scores show markedly different behavioral profiles in how they maintain and modify memories over time, revealing differences that aggregate accuracy masks.
AI.conclusion: MemProbe offers a reusable, cognitively inspired framework that turns aggregate performance metrics into interpretable behavioral profiles of agent memory maintenance, enabling finer-grained diagnosis of stability-plasticity tradeoffs in long-term memory systems.

title: Learning What to Skip: Counterfactual Credit Assignment for Efficient Multi-Agent LLM Workflows
summary: Multi-agent LLM workflows use planning, execution, verification, and summarization to improve task performance, yet the value of each component depends on the state already produced. Executing every component can waste computation or overwrite a correct intermediate answer. We formulate component omission as counterfactual credit assignment: full-workflow logs reveal the executed trajectory's reward, while controlled skip interventions reveal the consequences of omitting a future step. We introduce Learning What to Skip (LW2S), which learns action-specific safety models from these interventions and combines held-out calibration with domain-native guards to select skips. When an early skip is rejected, the controller can continue execution and reconsider a later component. Across mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice QA, and code generation with two instruction-model families, LW2S reduces recorded token cost while matching or improving aggregate full-workflow accuracy in the evaluated settings. Scale-up and second-topology experiments further examine component redundancy, while shared-error cases reveal why agreement alone is insufficient for skip selection. These findings connect efficient workflow execution to learning the conditional utility of individual components.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a method, LW2S, to learn when to skip components (steps) in multi-agent LLM workflows to save computation while preserving or improving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Existing multi-agent LLM workflows run all components (planning, execution, verification, summarization) every time. This can be wasteful because some steps may be unnecessary or even harmful when the current intermediate state is already good. There is a need to reason about the utility of each component conditioned on what has already happened and to avoid redundant or detrimental computation.
AI.method: They cast the decision of skipping components as a counterfactual credit assignment problem. Using full workflow execution logs, they obtain rewards for complete trajectories. Then they perform controlled interventions where future components are skipped to observe performance changes, allowing them to estimate the effect of omitting each step. Based on this, they propose Learning What to Skip (LW2S), which trains action-specific safety models that predict whether skipping a given component is safe. LW2S uses held-out calibration and domain-native guardrails to decide on skips at run time, with the controller allowed to resume the workflow and reconsider skipping later steps if an earlier skip is rejected.
AI.result: On benchmarks in mathematical reasoning, multiple-choice QA, and code generation, and across two instruction-tuned LLM families, LW2S lowers the overall token usage compared to always running the full workflow while matching or improving the full workflow’s accuracy. Additional experiments involving scaling and alternative workflow topologies analyze which components are redundant and show that mere agreement between agents is not a reliable criterion for skipping, due to shared errors.
AI.conclusion: Learning conditional, component-level utility enables more efficient LLM workflows: systems can skip unnecessary steps without degrading performance. LW2S provides a practical, data-driven way to implement such selective execution via counterfactual interventions and safety models, highlighting that smart control over workflow components can unlock significant savings in token cost while maintaining or improving task success.

title: Toward AI-Augmented Cooperative Engineering Workflows: Requirements and Architecture the European Rover Challenge
summary: The growing availability of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools creates new opportunities to support engineering design processes, yet their current use often remains limited to isolated tasks such as coding, documentation, or information retrieval. Less attention has been given to how AI can support cooperative engineering workflows at the process level, where teams must coordinate requirements, tasks, communication, knowledge transfer, and subsystem integration. This paper investigates this challenge in the context of the European Rover Challenge (ERC), where student teams design and integrate complex rover systems within a single academic cycle under strict time constraints and high subsystem interdependence. We conducted a role adaptive 40 question survey with ERC 2025 teams, yielding 104 responses from 14 teams. The survey examined team structure, knowledge transfer, task management, integration practices, communication patterns, and current AI usage. The results reveal recurring workflow bottlenecks, including limited documentation, unclear requirements, fragmented communication, informal task monitoring, and substantial integration rework. Based on these findings, we derive requirements for AI augmented cooperative engineering work-flows and propose an initial assistant system architecture that connects user facing interfaces, credential management, service selection, specialized AI services, and external engineering tools. The proposed architecture aims to support task clarification, requirement and compliance management, communication summarization, integration risk detection, and continuous knowledge capture. In doing so, the paper contributes empirical requirements and an architectural direction for AI augmented cooperative engineering workflows in hybrid human AI team settings.

AI.tldr: Survey-based study of student rover teams identifies workflow bottlenecks and proposes an AI-augmented architecture to support cooperative engineering processes.
AI.motivation: AI is increasingly used in engineering, but mainly for isolated tasks (coding, documentation, search). There is a gap in understanding and designing how AI can support end-to-end cooperative engineering workflows, where coordination, knowledge transfer, and subsystem integration are critical, especially under time pressure and high system complexity such as in student rover competitions.
AI.method: The authors conducted a role-adaptive, 40-question survey with European Rover Challenge 2025 student teams. They collected 104 responses from 14 teams, covering aspects like team structure, knowledge transfer, task and integration management, communication practices, and current AI usage. They analyzed recurring problems and translated them into requirements for AI support at the workflow level.
AI.result: The survey uncovered common bottlenecks across teams: poor or insufficient documentation, unclear or evolving requirements, fragmented and informal communication channels, ad hoc task tracking, and substantial rework during subsystem integration. From these findings, the authors extracted functional requirements for AI tools that go beyond single-task support to assist coordination and integration in team workflows.
AI.conclusion: Using the empirical findings from ERC rover teams, the paper defines requirements for AI-augmented cooperative engineering workflows and proposes an initial system architecture. This architecture links user interfaces, credential and service management, specialized AI services, and external engineering tools to enable features like task clarification, requirements and compliance support, communication summarization, integration risk detection, and continuous knowledge capture. The work offers both an evidence-based problem characterization and a concrete architectural direction for hybrid human–AI engineering teams.

title: Can Linguistic Reasoning Vectors Enhance Multimodal Reasoning Ability?
summary: Most Vision-Language Models (VLMs) are built by extending pretrained Large Language Models (LLMs) with visual modules and multimodal alignment. However, this multimodal scaling often degrades the language-side reasoning ability originally encoded in the base LLM. While the base LLM retains usable reasoning after scaling, the aligned VLM itself cannot reliably access this ability. Therefore, recovering the degraded reasoning capability in VLMs would benefit more from seeking help from the base LLM than from the VLM alone. Motivated by this, we propose LIFT (Language-side reasonIng Facilitation and Transfer), a lightweight vector-intervention method that transfers reasoning capability from the base LLM to the VLM without retraining the backbone. LIFT defines Reasoning Vectors as answer-token hidden-state differences between a Reasoner path with an explicit reasoning trace and a Solver path without it, and injects these vectors into language-side activations of the target VLM. LIFT further supports learnable vector adaptation while keeping the VLM backbone frozen. We evaluate LIFT on two VLMs across six reasoning benchmarks, comparing Reasoning Vectors extracted from the base LLM and from the aligned VLM under matched protocols. Results show that LLM-derived vectors consistently outperform VLM-derived vectors, confirming that the base LLM is a more effective source for recovering reasoning. LIFT partially recovers degraded reasoning through lightweight language-side interventions. Further analyses show that Reasoning Vectors influence intermediate reasoning behavior rather than merely altering final answers. The source code will be released soon.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces LIFT, a lightweight method to restore and enhance reasoning in Vision-Language Models by transferring reasoning behavior from the original base LLM via vector interventions, without retraining the VLM backbone.
AI.motivation: Extending pretrained LLMs into VLMs with visual modules and multimodal alignment often deteriorates the strong language reasoning abilities of the original LLM. Existing aligned VLMs cannot reliably access the reasoning competence that still resides in the base LLM. The paper is motivated by the need to recover or re-enable this degraded reasoning in VLMs in a simple, training-free or low-cost way, and by the hypothesis that the base LLM is a better reasoning source than the VLM itself.
AI.method: The authors propose LIFT (Language-side reasonIng Facilitation and Transfer), a vector-intervention mechanism applied at the language side of a VLM. They define Reasoning Vectors as the difference between hidden states of answer tokens under two prompting paths in the base model (or the VLM): a Reasoner path with explicit chain-of-thought reasoning and a Solver path with direct answering. These difference vectors are then injected into the target VLM’s language activations to encourage reasoning-like behavior, with optional learnable adaptation of the vectors. Crucially, this is done without retraining or modifying the VLM backbone weights.
AI.result: Across two different VLMs and six reasoning benchmarks, Reasoning Vectors derived from the base LLM consistently yield larger reasoning improvements than those derived from the aligned VLM under the same protocol. The method partially restores the degraded reasoning capabilities of the VLM with lightweight interventions. Analysis shows that LIFT affects intermediate reasoning trajectories rather than just flipping final outputs, indicating genuine reasoning facilitation rather than superficial answer biasing.
AI.conclusion: LIFT demonstrates that the base LLM underlying a VLM remains a superior source of reasoning behavior and that this capability can be transferred back to the VLM using simple vector interventions on language activations, without retraining. The approach partially recovers reasoning performance and appears to modify intermediate reasoning behavior, providing a practical path toward restoring lost language reasoning in multimodal models.

title: Momentum-Guided Federated Split Distillation for Personalized Temporal Edge Intelligence
summary: We propose a momentum-guided federated split distillation framework for personalized, efficient, and autonomous temporal edge intelligence. We introduce TeRR-SAtt, our novel temporal reservoir student attention design that combines fixed reservoir representations, a lightweight temporal student, and personalized output modules. We also present AMGF, our anticipatory momentum-guided fusion mechanism that clusters clients through learning momentum and derives specialized teacher updates. On real-world smart-building data, TeRR-SAtt reduces edge training latency by 65.50%, inference latency by 44.70%, training memory usage by 18.40%, and inference CPU usage by 33.10% over the considered baselines. At the same time, AMGF improves local learning by up to 35.31% in RMSE compared to global updates.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a momentum-guided federated split distillation framework with a new temporal attention module and a momentum-based client clustering mechanism, achieving significantly reduced edge resource usage and better personalized performance on temporal prediction tasks.
AI.motivation: Edge devices in temporal applications (like smart buildings) need personalized models that are accurate yet lightweight, with minimal training and inference cost. Standard federated learning with global models struggles with client heterogeneity, temporal dynamics, and limited edge resources, leading to suboptimal accuracy and high latency/resource usage.
AI.method: They design a federated split distillation framework where part of the model is shared and part is personalized. The main components are: (1) TeRR-SAtt, a temporal reservoir student attention module that uses fixed reservoir representations to capture temporal structure, a lightweight student network to learn from them, and client-specific output heads for personalization; (2) AMGF, an anticipatory momentum-guided fusion mechanism that uses clients' learning momentum to cluster them and derive specialized teacher updates instead of a single global model. This supports personalized temporal modeling with reduced computation and communication at the edge.
AI.result: On real smart-building datasets, their framework substantially reduces resource consumption compared to baselines: 65.50% lower edge training latency, 44.70% lower inference latency, 18.40% less training memory, and 33.10% less inference CPU usage. In addition, the AMGF fusion strategy improves local learning quality, with up to 35.31% reduction in RMSE versus standard global updates.
AI.conclusion: By combining temporal reservoir-based attention with momentum-guided federated fusion and split distillation, the proposed framework enables efficient, personalized temporal edge intelligence. It significantly cuts computation and resource usage on edge devices while improving prediction accuracy compared to conventional global federated learning approaches.

title: Neural State Prediction: Obstructing Shortcut Learning in EEG Foundation Models
summary: EEG foundation models increasingly use masked prediction to learn from unlabeled recordings, but optimizing this objective does not ensure transferable neural representations. A central challenge is that stable positional cues and local correlations can make masked regions predictable without integrating distributed neural context. To reduce this reliance on low-information prediction paths, we introduce Neural State Prediction (NSP), a latent-predictive framework that constrains both the prediction target and the available context. NSP uses a Target Encoder updated by an exponential moving average (EMA) to define latent supervision. Identity residualization removes additive effects associated with channel identity and relative time from the targets, while topology-separated context excludes their immediate spatial and temporal neighborhood from the visible input. We pretrain NSP on 2.2 million EEG segments from TUEG and evaluate it across 30 downstream datasets spanning clinical diagnosis, sleep staging, emotion recognition, motor imagery, event-related potentials, cognitive-state decoding, and language retrieval. Under full-parameter multi-task fine-tuning on EEG-FM-Bench, NSP achieves 63.94 macro balanced accuracy across 14 datasets, exceeding the strongest evaluated baseline by 2.35 percentage points. Controlled component ablations assess the contribution of each mechanism, while matched context controls and held-out interventions characterize the role of context geometry, signal content, and positional information. Jointly designing latent targets and their context offers a promising direction for EEG foundation models that learn from distributed signal structure.

AI.tldr: They propose a new self-supervised objective, Neural State Prediction (NSP), for EEG foundation models that encourages learning distributed neural representations rather than relying on trivial positional or local cues, and show it improves performance across many downstream EEG tasks.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG foundation models that use masked prediction can achieve low training loss by exploiting stable positional information and strong local correlations, without truly modeling the distributed neural dynamics. This leads to weakly transferable representations for a wide range of downstream tasks. The authors aim to design a pretraining objective that forces the model to integrate broader neural context and capture meaningful brain states, improving generalization across diverse EEG applications.
AI.method: They introduce Neural State Prediction (NSP), a latent-predictive framework for self-supervised EEG pretraining. NSP uses a separate Target Encoder, updated with an exponential moving average, to generate latent targets from EEG segments. Before supervision, the latent targets are processed with identity residualization to strip out additive components tied to electrode (channel) identity and relative time, reducing trivial positional information. On the input side, topology-separated context is enforced, meaning that for each prediction the model cannot see the immediate spatial and temporal neighborhood of the target, limiting easy local correlations as shortcuts. The base encoder is trained to predict the residualized latent target from this restricted context. They pretrain on 2.2M EEG segments from TUEG and then perform full-parameter multi-task fine-tuning on the EEG-FM-Bench benchmark, along with controlled ablations and interventions to analyze the contribution of each design choice.
AI.result: On EEG-FM-Bench, a multi-dataset benchmark comprising 14 EEG datasets, models pretrained with NSP and fully fine-tuned in a multi-task setting achieve 63.94 macro balanced accuracy, outperforming the strongest baseline by 2.35 percentage points. The authors also run component ablations showing that each mechanism—EMA target encoder, identity residualization, and topology-separated context—contributes to performance, and they conduct matched context controls and held-out interventions to dissect how context geometry, signal content, and positional information affect learning. Overall, the results indicate that NSP leads to more transferable representations compared to standard masked prediction approaches.
AI.conclusion: By jointly constraining both what is predicted (latent targets) and from where it is predicted (restricted, topology-aware context), Neural State Prediction reduces reliance on low-information shortcuts like positional and local correlations and promotes learning of distributed EEG signal structure. This results in better performance across a wide range of downstream EEG tasks, suggesting that carefully designing latent supervision and context geometry is a promising path for future EEG foundation models and possibly other time-series modalities.

title: Semantic Navigation for Issue Localization in Code Repository
summary: Repository-level issue localization aims to identify and rank the files and functions relevant to resolving a reported issue. LLM agents approach this task iteratively: they identify a set of potentially relevant locations, inspect the corresponding code, and revise their judgments about these candidates as new evidence is acquired. Existing environments, however, provide limited support for this loop: agents must search for unresolved relation targets, reconstruct entity semantics from raw source code, and revise candidates without evidential basis. To address these limitations, we present SemNav, a framework that leverages deterministic retrieval to seed a broad candidate set and an LLM agent to continually refine that set, thereby combining initial coverage with evidence-guided revision. SemNav supports this process through three key components. A Semantic Navigation Graph resolves program relations on demand through a language server, enabling direct navigation to related entities across files. Issue-conditioned Semantic Cards provide compact, source-grounded interpretations of each entity's role and relevance to the issue. A persistent Candidate Workspace records each candidate together with its evidential basis, enabling grounded verification, revision, and ranking. Across SWE-bench Lite and PLocBench, SemNav outperforms existing baselines, improving File Hit@10 from 68.33\% to 82.67\% with Gemma 4B. Component ablations and trajectory analysis support the complementary roles of all three components, while Semantic Cards reduce working-context load by 48.2\% relative to full-source reading. SemNav further ranks first on all seven evidence-quality metrics on SWE-Explore and improves downstream issue resolution from 44.00\% to 52.33\%.

AI.tldr: SemNav is a framework that enhances LLM-based repository-level issue localization by combining deterministic retrieval with agentic, evidence-guided refinement over a semantic navigation graph, semantic cards, and a candidate workspace, significantly improving localization accuracy, evidence quality, and issue resolution rates.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM agents for repository-level issue localization must manually reconstruct program structure from raw code and revise candidates without explicit, structured evidence, leading to inefficient navigation, high context load, and weaker localization performance. There is a need for an environment that explicitly represents program relations, provides concise, issue-conditioned summaries of entities, and tracks candidates together with their evidential basis to support iterative, evidence-guided reasoning.
AI.method: The authors propose SemNav, a framework with three main components: (1) a Semantic Navigation Graph that uses a language server to resolve program relations and enable direct, on-demand navigation across files and entities; (2) Issue-conditioned Semantic Cards that provide compact, source-grounded summaries of each entity’s semantics and its relevance to the issue; and (3) a persistent Candidate Workspace that stores candidate entities along with their supporting evidence, enabling grounded verification, revision, and ranking. Deterministic retrieval seeds an initial broad candidate set, and an LLM agent iteratively refines this set using the semantic graph, cards, and workspace.
AI.result: On benchmarks SWE-bench Lite and PLocBench, SemNav with Gemma 4B improves File Hit@10 from 68.33% to 82.67% over existing baselines. Ablation studies and trajectory analyses show that all three components contribute complementary benefits, and that Semantic Cards reduce working-context load by 48.2% compared to reading full source files. On SWE-Explore, SemNav achieves the best scores on all seven evidence-quality metrics and increases downstream issue resolution accuracy from 44.00% to 52.33%.
AI.conclusion: SemNav effectively supports LLM agents in repository-level issue localization by providing structured semantic navigation, concise issue-conditioned representations, and evidence-tracked candidate management. This design improves localization accuracy, reduces context usage, enhances evidence quality, and ultimately yields better automated issue resolution performance than prior approaches.

title: SPO: Discovering Adaptive Large Neighborhood Search Operators via Stackelberg Program Optimization
summary: Large neighborhood search (LNS) relies critically on destroy and repair operators, whose effectiveness depends on both adaptation to the evolving LNS state and interaction between the two roles.
