We introduce Stackelberg Program Optimization (SPO), an LLM-based framework for discovering adaptive executable destroy-repair programs. SPO conditions operator decisions on a compact LNS state, allowing state-dependent behavior to emerge through program discovery, and organizes destroy-repair discovery as a Stackelberg interaction over program space that reflects their asymmetric dependency. Role-specific credits evaluate destroy programs as leaders and repair programs as conditional follower responses, guiding a coupled optimization process that combines LLM generator learning with population-based evolutionary search over programs. Experiments on the traveling salesperson problem and capacitated vehicle routing problem show that SPO outperforms strong baselines across a broad range of settings and generalizes beyond the discovery scale to larger instances and benchmark sets. Behavioral analyses further demonstrate state-dependent operator behavior and coupled destroy-repair improvement during discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Stackelberg Program Optimization (SPO), an LLM-based framework that automatically discovers adaptive destroy-repair programs for Large Neighborhood Search, improving performance and generalization on TSP and CVRP.
AI.motivation: In Large Neighborhood Search, the quality of solutions strongly depends on the design of destroy and repair operators. Manually designing or tuning these operators so that they adapt to the evolving search state and interact effectively is difficult and problem-specific. Existing approaches often lack systematic mechanisms to model the asymmetric dependency between destroy and repair roles and to let operators adapt their behavior to the search state. With the rise of LLMs as programmable components, there is an opportunity to automatically discover and optimize such operators as executable programs instead of handcrafting them.
AI.method: The authors introduce Stackelberg Program Optimization (SPO), where destroy and repair operators are represented as executable programs generated and optimized using large language models. SPO conditions these program decisions on a compact representation of the LNS state, enabling state-dependent behavior. The discovery of operators is framed as a Stackelberg game: destroy operators act as leaders, and repair operators as followers that respond conditionally to the leaders’ behavior. Role-specific credit assignment evaluates destroy programs based on their leadership effect and repair programs based on their conditional performance, enabling a coupled optimization process. This process combines LLM generator training with population-based evolutionary search over program candidates, iteratively refining both destroy and repair programs.
AI.result: Through experiments on the traveling salesperson problem (TSP) and the capacitated vehicle routing problem (CVRP), SPO is shown to outperform strong baseline methods across a variety of experimental conditions. The learned destroy-repair programs generalize beyond the scale on which they were discovered, performing well on larger problem instances and standard benchmark sets. Empirical behavioral analyses indicate that the discovered operators exhibit meaningful state-dependent adaptations and demonstrate coupled improvement of destroy and repair behaviors over the course of the discovery process.
AI.conclusion: SPO offers an effective framework for automatically discovering adaptive, executable destroy-repair programs for Large Neighborhood Search using LLMs. By modeling the interaction of destroy and repair as a Stackelberg game and conditioning operators on LNS state, the method yields operators that both adapt to search dynamics and coordinate effectively. The approach improves solution quality on classic routing problems and generalizes to larger and benchmark instances, suggesting that LLM-based program optimization is a promising direction for automated design of heuristic components in combinatorial optimization.

title: Accounting for Bias Enables Sustainable LLM Evaluation
comment: 8 pages, 2 figures; SuRE'26: Workshop on Sustainability and Resource-Efficiency of Artificial Intelligence at IJCAI-ECAI 2026
summary: LLM-as-a-judge has become the de facto standard for scalable, subjective evaluation, yet current leaderboards compensate for systematic measurement bias by running ever more comparisons, an approach that is both statistically unsound and computationally wasteful. The root cause is an incomplete measurement model, treating LLM judges as neutral, interchangeable instruments ignores documented biases like position bias, verbosity bias, judge severity, and self-enhancement, that no volume of additional data can eliminate. We propose a unified latent variable framework that jointly models pairwise and ordinal data while explicitly correcting for these confounders, recovering reliable rankings from substantially fewer comparisons. Because fitting this model costs negligible compute relative to a single round of LLM inference, bias correction is not only more statistically rigorous but also a more sustainable approach to trustworthy evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that current LLM-as-a-judge leaderboards are statistically flawed and wasteful because they ignore systematic judge biases, and proposes a unified latent variable model that corrects these biases to obtain reliable rankings with fewer comparisons.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-as-a-judge evaluations and leaderboards rely on running many pairwise comparisons to average out biases, but this is both computationally expensive and statistically inadequate. Documented biases such as position bias, verbosity bias, judge severity, and self-enhancement distort results, and simply adding more data cannot fix a misspecified measurement model. There is a need for a principled, efficient, and statistically sound way to account for these confounders and yield trustworthy rankings of systems.
AI.method: The authors introduce a unified latent variable framework that simultaneously handles pairwise and ordinal preference data while explicitly modeling known LLM-judge biases. The model incorporates latent traits for systems and judges, as well as parameters capturing position bias, verbosity bias, judge severity, and self-enhancement effects. By fitting this model to the observed comparison data, they infer bias-corrected latent scores and rankings. The approach focuses on statistical estimation rather than more LLM calls, with model fitting being computationally cheap compared to LLM inference.
AI.result: Using the proposed latent variable framework, the authors can recover more reliable and stable rankings of systems with substantially fewer pairwise comparisons than existing leaderboard methodologies require. The model successfully adjusts for systematic biases of LLM judges, leading to evaluations that better reflect underlying system quality instead of artifacts of the judging process. They demonstrate that the computational overhead of bias correction is negligible compared to the cost of additional LLM inference, making their approach both cost-effective and scalable.
AI.conclusion: Bias in LLM-as-a-judge evaluations cannot be eliminated by simply increasing the number of comparisons; it requires an explicitly specified measurement model. The proposed unified latent variable framework provides a statistically principled and computationally efficient way to correct for key biases like position, verbosity, severity, and self-enhancement. As a result, it enables more trustworthy, sustainable, and data-efficient evaluation and leaderboard construction for LLM systems.

title: Evolutionary Safety of Recursive Self-Improving AI: Taxonomy, Risk Discovery, and Evaluation
summary:
Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly, with increasingly capable systems taking larger roles in reasoning, decision-making, scientific discovery, and autonomous development. As AI begins to participate in its own improvement, from model training and experience accumulation to agent evolution and automated AI development, the prospect of recursive self-improvement (RSI) is becoming increasingly relevant. This transition raises a fundamental safety question: how can safety be maintained when the system, its accumulated experience, and even the process producing its successors continue to change?
  We introduce Evolutionary Safety as a perspective for studying safety under persistent and recursive self-improvement. It concerns not only whether an AI system is safe at a particular moment, but how safety properties change, persist, accumulate, and propagate throughout evolution. We characterize recurring manifestations, including intent drift, error accumulation, experience contamination, safety-property erosion, evaluator drift, and risk propagation. We then develop a taxonomy spanning persistent agent state, model state, evaluation and environmental feedback, computational substrate, and meta-level update mechanisms. Building on this taxonomy, we examine how evolutionary risks can be discovered and evaluated across states, updates, trajectories, and lineages, and derive governance principles for modification, selection, authorization, provenance, and recovery. Finally, we outline open problems toward maintaining safety guarantees as AI systems become increasingly persistent, adaptive, and recursively self-improving. Project resources and proposed evaluation systems are available at https://chaunceykung.github.io/evolutionary-safety-rsi.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a new framework, Evolutionary Safety, for understanding and managing safety in AI systems that continually and recursively improve themselves.
AI.motivation: Current AI safety work mostly evaluates systems at a fixed point in time, assuming relatively static models and deployment conditions. As AI systems become more persistent, autonomous, and involved in their own improvement—via continuous training, agent evolution, and automated AI development—this snapshot view is insufficient. The authors are motivated by the need to understand how safety can be preserved when both the AI system and the processes that modify or replace it are constantly changing, raising concerns like intent drift, accumulating errors, and uncontrolled propagation of risks across AI generations.
AI.method: The authors introduce the concept of Evolutionary Safety and construct a conceptual and analytical framework rather than an empirical one. They (1) identify and formalize recurring safety issues in recursively self-improving systems—such as intent drift, error accumulation, experience contamination, safety-property erosion, evaluator drift, and risk propagation; (2) develop a taxonomy of where and how these risks arise, structured around persistent agent state, model state, evaluation and environmental feedback, computational substrate, and meta-level update mechanisms; and (3) use this taxonomy to propose ways to detect and measure evolutionary risks across states, updates, trajectories, and lineages, and to derive governance principles for controlling modification, selection, authorization, provenance, and recovery in RSI-capable systems.
AI.result: The main result is a structured theoretical framework and taxonomy for reasoning about safety in recursively self-improving AI systems. The paper clarifies distinct types of evolutionary safety risks, shows how they can manifest and propagate through different components and generations of AI systems, and articulates how evaluation might be extended from static models to evolving lineages. It also formulates governance principles aimed at keeping safety constraints intact as systems adapt and self-improve, and provides early-stage resources and proposed evaluation systems to begin operationalizing these ideas.
AI.conclusion: The paper concludes that maintaining safety for future, persistent, and recursively self-improving AI requires shifting focus from static, one-shot evaluations to an evolutionary perspective that tracks how safety properties change over time and across generations. By framing key risk patterns, providing a taxonomy, and articulating governance principles for modification, selection, authorization, provenance, and recovery, the authors lay groundwork for a research agenda on Evolutionary Safety. They highlight many open problems and argue that solving them is critical as AI systems take on larger roles in their own development and deployment.

title: Samples, Sources, Space: Decomposing Data Scale in Spatially Structured Representation Learning of Human Brain Microarchitecture
summary: Scaling studies typically represent training data by a single count of samples. For hierarchically and spatially structured data, however, the same number of samples can be drawn from few or many sources and distributed differently across the underlying domain. We therefore study data scaling as an allocation problem, separating unique sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage. We study this decomposition in microscopic whole-brain histology, where a source is an individual brain, and a sample is an image patch at a specific spatial location. Across 93 controlled pretraining runs of a contrastive model that uses spatial proximity for supervision, we vary data allocation, compute, and model capacity over 11.6 million spatially anchored image patches from 21 human brains. Performance improves with more unique samples, broader spatial coverage, additional compute, and larger model capacity. At fixed sample count, distributing samples across one to 18 subjects produces no detectable improvement, even though representations generalize substantially better to subjects encountered during pretraining. Inter-subject variation therefore strongly affects generalization, but additional subjects provide no benefit when a fixed sample budget is distributed across more sources. These results establish sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage as distinct axes of data scaling in spatially structured representation learning.

AI.tldr: They decompose data scaling in spatially structured tasks into three axes—unique samples, source diversity, and spatial coverage—and empirically show that, with a fixed sample budget, adding more brains (sources) does not improve performance, even though inter-subject variation matters for generalization.
AI.motivation: Standard scaling laws count only total samples, ignoring that in spatially and hierarchically structured domains the same sample count can be drawn from differing numbers of sources (e.g., subjects) and arranged differently over space. In applications like whole-brain histology, this overlooks crucial questions: Is it better to sample many locations per subject or fewer locations from many subjects? How do spatial coverage and subject diversity separately impact representation quality and generalization? The paper aims to disentangle these factors to guide data collection and model design in such settings.
AI.method: They formalize data scaling as an allocation problem with three components: (1) unique sample count, (2) source diversity (number of brains/subjects), and (3) spatial coverage (distribution of samples over anatomical space). Using microscopic whole-brain histology data, they treat each human brain as a source and each spatially localized image patch as a sample. They run 93 controlled pretraining experiments of a contrastive representation learning model that uses spatial proximity as the supervision signal. Across runs, they systematically vary: (a) how samples are allocated across brains and spatial locations, (b) total compute, and (c) model capacity, while keeping track of performance and generalization to unseen or seen subjects.
AI.result: Performance monotonically benefits from more unique samples, wider spatial coverage, more compute, and larger model capacity. However, when total sample count is held fixed, varying the number of brains from which samples are drawn (from 1 up to 18) produces no measurable performance gains. Despite this, the learned representations do generalize much better to subjects that were present during pretraining compared with completely new subjects, indicating strong inter-subject variation. Thus, subject diversity influences generalization properties, but within a fixed sample budget, spreading samples over additional subjects does not yield improved performance.
AI.conclusion: In spatially structured representation learning, data scaling is not fully captured by a single sample-count metric; instead, it has at least three distinct axes: sample count, source diversity, and spatial coverage. Their experiments in whole-brain histology show that scaling unique samples, spatial coverage, compute, and model capacity all help, while simply increasing the number of sources under a fixed sample budget does not. This has practical implications for experimental design: when data collection is constrained, it may be more beneficial to increase per-source sampling and spatial coverage than to add more sources, even though subject-level variability still critically shapes generalization behavior.

title: The Right Information Extraction Pipeline Depends on the Document: Accuracy-Energy Trade-offs for Small, Local Models
summary: Whether an information extraction pipeline should process page images or parsed text depends on the document, and the answer flips across the layout spectrum. We study this trade-off under a constraint that rules out (closed) cloud services: privacy-sensitive documents processed on-premise by small ($\le 8\mathrm{B}$ parameter) text-only and vision--language models, evaluated on both accuracy and energy over a design space spanning input representation, model family, and inference configuration. Benchmarking on the near-plain-text Kleister-NDA contracts and the layout-rich VRDU forms, we find that batching is the dominant energy lever, cutting energy per page by 38-85% at no cost in accuracy, while FP8 quantization saves 27-32% when requests are served one at a time but less than 1mWh per page (9-19%) once batching is applied. Preprocessing dominates what remains: neural OCR costs $17\times$ more energy per page than classical OCR and never reaches the Pareto frontier. Which representation wins flips with the type of document: vision--language models on layout-rich documents and small text-only models with a cheap parser on near-plain text, where they are both more accurate and cheaper than any vision--language configuration. Our work yields concrete guidelines for energy-efficient, privacy-compliant local information extraction.

AI.tldr: Study compares page-image vs parsed-text pipelines for on-premise information extraction using small text-only and vision–language models, jointly optimizing accuracy and energy.
AI.motivation: Organizations with privacy-sensitive documents must run information extraction locally without large cloud models, creating a need to understand when to use image-based vs text-based processing and how to minimize energy while preserving accuracy.
AI.method: Systematic benchmarking across a design space of input representations (image vs parsed text, different OCR types), model families (small text-only vs vision–language models ≤8B parameters), and inference configurations (batching levels, FP8 quantization), measured on two benchmarks with very different layout complexity: Kleister-NDA contracts and VRDU forms. Evaluate accuracy and per-page energy and construct Pareto frontiers.
AI.result: Batching is the main energy saver, reducing energy per page by 38–85% with no accuracy loss. FP8 quantization saves 27–32% energy in single-request scenarios but only 9–19% (<1 mWh/page) when batching is already used. Neural OCR is ~17× more energy-hungry than classical OCR and never Pareto-optimal. Representation choice flips by document type: vision–language models dominate on layout-rich forms, while small text-only models with cheap parsers are both more accurate and cheaper on near-plain-text contracts.
AI.conclusion: For privacy-compliant, local information extraction under small-model constraints, designers should aggressively batch requests, prefer classical OCR, and select representations based on layout: text-only pipelines for near-plain text and vision–language pipelines for layout-heavy documents. These principles provide concrete guidelines for building energy-efficient on-premise IE systems.

title: Which Influence Are We Estimating? The Role of Counterfactual Specifications in Data Attribution
summary: Estimating the influence of training examples on model behavior is essential for data debugging, valuation, and attribution. Existing influence estimators often produce incompatible rankings, which are commonly ascribed to approximation error. We argue that a more fundamental source of disagreement is specification mismatch: influence depends on the behavior being attributed, the intervention applied to each training example, and the counterfactual training process that maps the intervention to a model response. These choices are especially important when the target behavior requires a tractable surrogate, such as query loss, a logit, or a margin. We formalize influence as a counterfactual estimand, distinguish specification mismatch across estimands from approximation error in estimating a fixed estimand, and organize representative estimators by their implied specifications. We further derive a local decomposition that exposes how behavior signals, training signals, and counterfactual parameter responses interact. Controlled experiments show that exact estimands under different specifications can induce different rankings, whereas approximation error grows as perturbations move farther from their linearization points. Experiments on noisy label detection and LLM attribution show that specification choices significantly affect attribution quality, especially for the choice of behavior surrogate. Behavior-aligned specifications can identify target-specific training examples obscured by default loss-based or similarity-based specifications. These results establish specification analysis as a necessary first step for interpreting and comparing data influence estimators.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that disagreements among data influence estimators are mainly due to how influence is defined (its specification), not just approximation error, and shows that making the specification match the desired behavior is crucial for reliable attribution.
AI.motivation: Influence functions and related methods are widely used to understand which training examples drive specific model behaviors, for tasks like data debugging, valuation, and attribution. However, different influence estimators often give conflicting rankings of influential examples. This disagreement has typically been blamed on approximation error, but practitioners lack a principled framework to understand and reconcile these differences, especially when they must use surrogate behavior metrics (e.g., query loss, logits, margins) instead of the true downstream behavior of interest.
AI.method: The authors formalize data influence as a counterfactual estimand defined by three components: (1) the behavior being attributed, (2) the intervention on each training example, and (3) the counterfactual training process mapping interventions to model changes. They distinguish between (a) specification mismatch, where estimators target different estimands, and (b) approximation error, where an estimator imperfectly approximates a fixed estimand. They categorize common influence estimators by their implicit specifications and derive a local (linearized) decomposition showing how behavior signals, training signals, and parameter responses interact. They then conduct controlled experiments and practical case studies to empirically compare exact estimands under different specifications, and to quantify approximation error as perturbations move away from linearization points.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis shows that even exact influence estimands, when defined under different specifications (e.g., different behavior surrogates or interventions), can yield substantially different rankings of influential training examples. The local decomposition clarifies how behavior choice, training signals, and parameter responses combine, and highlights that behavior surrogates have a strong impact. Empirically, controlled experiments confirm that specification differences alone can cause divergent rankings, while approximation error increases with the magnitude of perturbations away from linear regimes. In noisy label detection and LLM attribution tasks, specification choices—especially the selection of behavior surrogate—significantly affect the quality of data attribution, with behavior-aligned specifications outperforming standard loss-based or similarity-based ones.
AI.conclusion: The main conclusion is that disagreements between influence estimators stem primarily from specification mismatch rather than just approximation error. Therefore, before choosing or comparing influence estimators, practitioners must explicitly specify the target behavior, intervention, and training counterfactual. Behavior-aligned specifications, particularly appropriate behavior surrogates, are critical for identifying the training examples that truly drive a given model behavior. The paper positions specification analysis as a necessary preliminary step for interpreting, designing, and evaluating data influence estimation methods.

title: Learning to Stop without Learning to Stop: Self-Supervised Confidence Training Improves Reasoning Efficiency
summary: Reasoning models often generate very long reasoning traces, making inference computationally expensive. Existing approaches typically improve efficiency either through inference-time early-stopping mechanisms or by explicitly encouraging shorter reasoning during training, for example through reinforcement learning with length penalties. We show that substantial efficiency gains can instead emerge from a different kind of supervision: \textit{confidence}. Using a self-supervised procedure, we fine-tune reasoning models to predict their confidence in the answer at intermediate points along their own reasoning trajectories using only 600 training problems. Confidence is used only as a training target: the loss contains no objective for reasoning length, efficiency, or stopping. At inference, the fine-tuned models use the standard generation procedure, with no confidence elicitation or early-stopping mechanism. Despite this, self-supervised confidence fine-tuning makes reasoning more efficient, reducing generated tokens by up to 25\% at matched accuracy across Gemma, Qwen, Nemotron, and GPT-OSS models on mathematical, scientific, and coding reasoning benchmarks, with efficiency gains comparable to methods that explicitly optimize for shorter reasoning. Analysis of reasoning episodes further shows that confidence supervision largely preserves the base models' high-level reasoning composition rather than selectively suppressing particular behaviors. Our results suggest that efficient reasoning may emerge as a downstream consequence of learning metacognitive signals, without being directly optimized.

AI.tldr: They fine-tune reasoning models to estimate their own confidence mid-chain and, surprisingly, this alone makes the models reason more efficiently (fewer tokens) at the same accuracy.
AI.motivation: Long chain-of-thought reasoning is computationally expensive; existing methods for improving efficiency require explicit control of reasoning length (e.g., early stopping or length penalties), which can be complex, task-specific, or hurt accuracy. The authors want a simpler, more general way to get efficient reasoning without directly optimizing for shortness.
AI.method: Use a self-supervised procedure where a reasoning model generates full reasoning traces on training problems, and then is fine-tuned to predict its confidence in the eventual answer at intermediate points along each reasoning trajectory. Confidence is the only auxiliary target; the loss does not include any objective involving reasoning length or stopping. Training uses only about 600 problems. At test time, the model is used with standard decoding—no explicit confidence querying or early-stopping mechanism is applied.
AI.result: Across multiple families of reasoning-focused LMs (Gemma, Qwen, Nemotron, GPT-OSS) and across math, science, and coding benchmarks, the confidence-fine-tuned models use up to 25% fewer generated tokens while matching the base models' accuracy. The efficiency gains are comparable to approaches that explicitly optimize for shorter chains of thought.
AI.conclusion: Teaching models to estimate their own confidence along reasoning trajectories can implicitly lead to more efficient reasoning, even without explicit pressure on length or early stopping. Confidence supervision appears to preserve the structure of the model's reasoning while making it more concise, indicating that metacognitive training signals can be a powerful indirect route to efficiency.

title: DIAL: Position-Debiased LLM Judges with Adaptive Human Preference Calibration
summary: Large language models (LLMs) as a judge enable scalable evaluation, but their judgments can be sensitive to response order and, even after removing such position effects, can still diverge systematically from human preferences.We introduce DIAL, a unified framework that combines abundant LLM comparisons with limited human comparisons to separate judge-specific position effects, learn shared structure in position-debiased LLM preferences, and adaptively calibrate that structure toward the human preference target. Theoretically, we study three aspects of DIAL: (i) identification of latent LLM preferences, position effects, and human calibration; (ii) adaptive estimation that balances LLM anchoring against limited human evidence; and (iii) fixed-weight uncertainty quantification for the calibrated human preference. Empirically, we evaluate position debiasing and human alignment separately in controlled simulations and on three human-preference benchmarks, showing that DIAL remains robust to unbalanced response order, achieves strong human-aligned rankings with limited labels, and adapts toward human evidence when LLM information is imperfect. Our real-data study collects over 410K judgments from 21 LLM judges in both display orders, providing a resource for future studies of LLM-judge bias, heterogeneity, and human alignment.

AI.tldr: DIAL is a framework that corrects LLM-judge biases and calibrates their preference rankings to match humans using many LLM comparisons plus a small number of human labels.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly used as automatic judges to evaluate other models or responses because this scales better than human evaluation. However, their judgments show systematic biases, such as sensitivity to which answer appears first (position effects), and even after simple de-biasing, they may still disagree with real human preferences in structured ways. There is a need for a principled method that can: (1) disentangle order/position bias from genuine underlying preferences, (2) exploit the large volume of cheap LLM-judge data while (3) using a relatively small amount of expensive human data to steer these preferences toward true human judgments, with theoretical guarantees.
AI.method: They propose DIAL, a unified statistical/learning framework that models: (a) latent position-independent preferences of each LLM judge, (b) judge-specific position effects (how each LLM is biased by response order), and (c) a calibration mapping from LLM preference structure to human preferences. DIAL uses pairwise comparison data where the same responses are shown in different orders to identify and remove position effects, then learns shared structure across many LLM judges to infer latent preference scores. Limited human comparison data is then used to adaptively calibrate these latent LLM-based preferences toward the human target, balancing reliance on LLM data vs human evidence. They analyze identifiability, propose an adaptive estimation procedure that trades off LLM anchoring vs human labels, and provide an uncertainty quantification scheme using fixed weights for the calibrated human preference estimates.
AI.result: Through simulations and experiments on three human-preference benchmarks, they show: (1) DIAL effectively removes position bias, remaining robust even when response orders are highly unbalanced; (2) it can recover rankings that align well with human preferences using only a limited number of human labels, leveraging abundant LLM comparison data; and (3) when LLM information is noisy or imperfect, the method naturally shifts weight toward the human data rather than being misled by flawed LLM judges. They also collect and release a large-scale dataset of over 410K pairwise judgments from 21 different LLM judges, each evaluated in both display orders, to enable further study.
AI.conclusion: DIAL provides a principled, unified way to debias and calibrate LLM-as-a-judge evaluations toward human preferences, combining the scalability of LLM judgments with the reliability of human labels. It is theoretically grounded (identification, adaptive estimation, uncertainty quantification) and empirically effective at correcting position effects and aligning to humans with few labels. The new dataset of multi-judge, dual-order comparisons offers a valuable resource for future work on understanding and mitigating LLM-judge biases and heterogeneity.

title: Purin: A Biology-inspired Mechanism for Artificial Neural Networks
summary: Artificial neural networks (ANNs) usually represent neural transmission with fixed trainable weights during a training batch, which omits short-term changes in synaptic efficacy. In addition, the discrete time-step simulation requires additional temporal processing that many conventional ANN architectures do not use. To overcome these challenges, we propose Purin, a biology-inspired and ANN-compatible mechanism, that introduces synaptic efficacy modulation into conventional convolutional neural networks. Purin uses a time-interval-based abstraction for neural activities, which allows Purin to introduce short- and long-term synaptic efficacy changes without using discrete time-steps. Purin introduces a bounded factor to represent temporary synaptic efficacy changes, together with two weight matrices that represent input-side and output-side efficacy. The weight matrices are updated by backpropagation and interpreted as the long-term synaptic efficacy changes. Experimental results show that after removing the confounding factors in the AlexNet, VGG11, and GoogLeNet architectures, Purin improves the classification accuracies in all three models across the evaluated datasets.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Purin, a biologically inspired mechanism that integrates short- and long-term synaptic efficacy modulation into standard CNNs using a time-interval abstraction instead of discrete time steps, leading to improved classification performance on multiple architectures and datasets.
AI.motivation: Conventional ANNs use fixed weights during each training batch, ignoring rapid short-term synaptic changes seen in biology, and they typically rely on discrete time-step simulations for temporal processing, which many architectures do not exploit. The authors aim to incorporate biologically plausible synaptic efficacy dynamics into standard CNNs without the overhead of explicit time-step modeling, to potentially improve learning and performance.
AI.method: The authors propose Purin, a mechanism that models neural activity over time intervals rather than discrete time steps. Purin introduces a bounded factor that captures temporary (short‑term) synaptic efficacy changes and augments each synapse with two learnable weight matrices: one for input-side efficacy and one for output-side efficacy. These matrices are trained via backpropagation and represent long-term synaptic efficacy changes. Purin is integrated into common CNN architectures (AlexNet, VGG11, GoogLeNet) in a way that remains compatible with standard ANN training pipelines.
AI.result: When incorporated into AlexNet, VGG11, and GoogLeNet, and after controlling for confounding architectural differences, Purin consistently improves image classification accuracy across the evaluated datasets compared to their respective baselines without Purin.
AI.conclusion: Purin successfully brings biologically inspired synaptic efficacy modulation into conventional CNNs using a time-interval abstraction that avoids discrete time-step simulations. This design allows simultaneous modeling of short- and long-term synaptic changes, is trainable with standard backpropagation, and yields measurable accuracy gains on several benchmark CNN architectures and datasets.

title: MA-WAM: Multi-Agent World-Action Model for Test-Time Planning
comment: 40 pages, including appendices. Project page: https://ma-wam.github.io/
summary: Multi-agent cooperative tasks require different agents to execute a joint action simultaneously, and each agent's action affects both the observations and responses of the other agents. Hence, a world model is needed to predict the team return resulting from the joint actions of all agents. A naive extension directly applies a single-agent world model to each agent's action when predicting the team return step by step. However, such an extension fails to capture the dependencies among the simultaneous actions of multiple agents. We propose Multi-Agent World-Action Model (MA-WAM), a test-time planning framework that enables a frozen multi-agent flow policy to evaluate futures of candidate joint actions. To our knowledge, MA-WAM is the first test-time world-model planner for multi-agent flow policies. MA-WAM predicts the consequences of each joint action according to cross-agent dependencies and enables efficient candidate scoring. Across 30 offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) settings on MAMuJoCo, SMAC, and MPE, MA-WAM achieves mean relative gains of 22.0% over direct execution and 25.6% over uniform action selection. Under the standard evaluation protocol on an A100 GPU, MA-WAM adds 12.1 ms, accounting for 2.5% of the measured generation-and-scoring time.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes MA-WAM, a multi-agent world-action model for test-time planning that accounts for cross-agent dependencies in joint actions, improving performance over naive baselines with minimal computational overhead.
AI.motivation: In multi-agent cooperative tasks, agents must take joint actions whose effects are interdependent, but naive world-model approaches treat each agent independently, failing to model cross-agent dependencies and leading to suboptimal planning and team returns.
AI.method: The authors introduce MA-WAM, a test-time planning framework built on top of a frozen multi-agent flow policy. MA-WAM uses a world-action model that predicts the consequences of joint actions by explicitly modeling cross-agent dependencies, enabling efficient scoring of candidate joint actions during planning without retraining the policy.
AI.result: On 30 offline MARL settings across MAMuJoCo, SMAC, and MPE benchmarks, MA-WAM yields mean relative performance gains of 22.0% over directly executing the learned policy and 25.6% over uniformly selecting actions, while incurring only 12.1 ms additional computation (about 2.5% of overall generation-and-scoring time) on an A100 GPU under standard evaluation protocols.
AI.conclusion: MA-WAM effectively enables test-time world-model planning for multi-agent flow policies by accurately modeling the joint consequences of agents’ actions, substantially improving cooperative multi-agent task performance with minimal computational overhead.

title: G2MAF: Test-Time Gradient Guidance for Multi-Agent Flow Policies
comment: 24 pages, including appendices. Project page: https://g2maf.github.io/
summary: Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) learns cooperative policies from fixed datasets without further environment interaction and a learned policy is frozen at deployment. Such a frozen policy typically proposes a single joint action and executes it directly at deployment time. However, this one-shot deployment often commits to a suboptimal proposal, even when better nearby alternatives remain consistent with the behavior data. To address this issue, we propose Gradient Guided Multi Agent Flow (G2MAF), a refinement framework for optimizing joint policies at test-time. G2MAF applies one globally normalized, projected critic gradient to guide and coordinate all agents' corrections while keeping the action both feasible and close to the frozen policy proposal. Across 24 MPE and SMAC settings, its canonical variant improves 20 frozen settings, with mean relative gains of 9.2% on MPE and 8.9% on SMAC, with model inference latency increased by about 6% only.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces G2MAF, a test-time refinement framework that improves offline multi-agent RL policies by applying a single coordinated critic gradient step to adjust joint actions while staying close to a frozen policy, achieving ~9% performance gains with minimal extra latency.
AI.motivation: Offline MARL policies are frozen at deployment and select one-shot joint actions that can be suboptimal, even when better nearby actions are still supported by the dataset. There is a need for a mechanism to improve these frozen policies at test time without additional environment interaction, by exploiting local structure in the learned critic and remaining consistent with offline data constraints.
AI.method: The paper proposes Gradient Guided Multi Agent Flow (G2MAF), which refines the frozen joint action at test time using the critic’s gradient. It computes a globally normalized, projected gradient from the learned critic and applies it to all agents’ actions simultaneously, coordinating their corrections. The update is constrained so that the refined action remains feasible and close to the original frozen proposal, effectively performing a single, low-cost test-time optimization step per decision.
AI.result: In experiments on 24 tasks across the MPE and SMAC benchmarks, the canonical G2MAF variant improves the performance of 20 frozen offline MARL settings. The reported mean relative performance gains are 9.2% on MPE and 8.9% on SMAC, while model inference latency increases by only about 6%, indicating that the refinement adds modest computational overhead.
AI.conclusion: Test-time refinement of offline MARL joint actions via a single, globally coordinated critic gradient step can substantially improve performance over frozen policies with minimal inference cost. G2MAF shows that locally optimizing actions around the frozen proposal—while respecting feasibility and staying close to the original actions—is an effective strategy for leveraging offline critics more fully at deployment.

title: Mutable Transcripts: Mitigating Context Pollution through Editable Conversation State
summary: Contemporary large language model (LLM) chat systems treat conversation history as an immutable sequence of turns that defines the model's working context. However, user intent in real interactions is not static: it evolves through correction, refinement, and shifting constraints. This mismatch between dynamic intent and static transcripts can result in context pollution, where outdated or irrelevant information persists and continues to influence subsequent responses. We introduce mutable transcripts, a new interaction paradigm that enables users to revise prior turns through natural language edit requests, allowing the conversation history itself to be updated rather than appended. This reframes the transcript from a passive record into an editable representation of conversational state. We present a working prototype that integrates transcript-level revision into a standard chat interface and evaluate its feasibility through a controlled user study (n=17) and an illustrative transcript analysis of representative interaction scenarios. Participants significantly preferred mutable transcripts over standard chat across measures of clarity, confidence, and ease of use, with reduced intent to restart conversations. Transcript analysis of representative user study conversations shows that mutable transcripts can reduce conversation length and eliminate obsolete retained context. These findings provide initial evidence that user-driven revision of conversational history can improve interaction quality and help maintain a more current representation of user intent. The source code and prototype can be accessed at https://github.com/QxLabIreland/ReChat

AI.tldr: The paper proposes “mutable transcripts” for LLM chat, where users can edit past turns via natural language so the conversation state updates instead of only appending new messages. A prototype and user study show this reduces obsolete context, shortens conversations, and improves perceived clarity and ease of use compared to standard chat.
AI.motivation: Current LLM chat treats the dialogue history as an unchangeable log, but in realistic use, users frequently correct or refine their goals. When old, now-wrong information remains in the context, it can pollute the model’s behavior, forcing users to restart chats or fight against the history. The authors aim to better align the interaction model with evolving user intent and reduce negative effects of stale or incorrect context.
AI.method: They introduce the concept of “mutable transcripts,” where earlier turns can be revised through natural language edit requests that rewrite the stored transcript rather than append corrections. They built a prototype chat interface implementing this idea and ran a controlled user study with 17 participants comparing mutable transcripts to standard chat. They also conducted qualitative transcript analysis of representative interactions to understand how edits affected conversation flow and context retention.
AI.result: Participants significantly preferred mutable transcripts across several subjective measures, including clarity of the conversation, confidence in system behavior, and ease of use, and they expressed less desire to restart conversations. The transcript analysis showed that mutable transcripts led to shorter conversations and removed obsolete or incorrect context that would otherwise persist in traditional chat logs.
AI.conclusion: Allowing users to directly revise conversation history via mutable transcripts can better maintain an up-to-date representation of user intent and improve the overall quality of LLM interactions. Early evidence from a prototype and small-scale user study suggests this paradigm mitigates context pollution, reduces unnecessary dialogue length, and is preferred by users over standard immutable chat interfaces.

title: Programs-of-Layers in LLMs through the Lens of Cortical Areas
summary: Inference in LLMs is conventionally a fixed-depth, fixed-order forward pass through every layer, regardless of how difficult the input is. The human brain does not work this way: using the thalamus as a central hub, it routes information flexibly to all regions of the cortex according to demand. Li et al. (2026) recently showed, with a system they call program-of-layers (PoLar), that transformers can be given an analogous flexibility if their layers are treated as a library of functions rather than a fixed sequence. Performance improves over the standard forward pass when each input is dynamically routed through an adaptive sequence of skipped or repeated contiguous layer blocks. We reconstructed PoLar's diagnostic MCTS in more detail than the original paper and applied it across 5 models. We reproduced several of PoLar's findings: skipping outperformed the standard pass, repeating outperformed skipping, and combining both outperformed either alone. Shorter programs sufficed for easier questions, while harder questions required more layer repeats. However, we failed to replicate the main claim regarding their learned router for single-shot inference: its top-ranked prediction consistently collapsed back to the standard pass, even though its top-k predicted programs, taken together, did show a real accuracy gain. Beyond reproduction, we find that a small number of generic programs are enough to solve most of the questions. We also provide a much deeper analysis of these programs' structure and robustness: for example, we found that programs that correct errors are highly brittle: undoing even a single edit inside a program typically breaks the correction. Connecting this to the brain's routing mechanisms, PoLar mirrors principles of thalamo-cortical coordination between cortical-area-like transformer layers. We publicly release the code at https://datexis.github.io/RE-PoLar/

AI.tldr: This paper re-examines PoLar, a method that dynamically routes inputs through transformer layers, confirming many benefits of adaptive routing but failing to reproduce the key claim that a learned router reliably beats the standard forward pass.
AI.motivation: Standard transformer inference runs every layer in a fixed order and depth, independent of input difficulty, unlike the brain’s flexible, demand-based routing via the thalamus. PoLar proposes treating layers as a function library and using dynamic routing to potentially improve efficiency and performance. This paper aims to carefully reproduce and stress-test PoLar’s claims, clarify what actually works, and better understand the structure and robustness of the resulting layer programs.
AI.method: The authors reconstruct PoLar’s Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) diagnostic procedure in more detail, then apply it across five language models. They compare different routing regimes: standard pass, skipping layer blocks, repeating layer blocks, and combining skipping and repeating into adaptive “programs of layers.” They test PoLar’s learned router for single-shot inference and analyze which discovered programs are used, how many are needed, their length versus question difficulty, and the brittleness of programs by perturbing individual edits. They also relate observed routing patterns to principles from thalamo-cortical coordination in neuroscience.
AI.result: They successfully reproduce core PoLar findings with diagnostic search: (1) skipping improves performance over the standard forward pass, (2) repeating improves over skipping, and (3) combining both yields the best gains; moreover, easier questions require shorter programs while harder questions benefit from more layer repetitions. However, they fail to replicate the central claim that PoLar’s learned router yields a superior single-shot top-1 program: in their experiments, the top-ranked routed program usually degenerates to the standard pass, though the whole top-k program set offers a genuine accuracy boost. They also discover that a small set of generic programs covers most questions and that error-correcting programs are extremely fragile, with single-program edits often destroying the correction effect.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive routing over transformer layers can indeed outperform the standard fixed-depth forward pass when searched or used in a top-k fashion, and only a modest repertoire of generic programs seems necessary in practice. However, PoLar’s learned router does not reliably realize these gains in its top-1 prediction and tends to collapse back to the standard forward pass. The discovered layer programs, especially those that fix model errors, are structurally brittle. These findings temper the original PoLar claims, sharpen our understanding of dynamic routing in transformers, and strengthen the conceptual analogy to thalamo-cortical routing in the brain. The authors release their implementation for further study.

title: Completed Pairs Hide Capped Failures: A ReVerPi Case Study of Selective Context Projection
comment: 15 pages, 12 tables, 5 figures. Project code: https://github.com/timwhitez/ReVer_Pi. Source archive includes anc/ analysis data and reproduction scripts
summary: Context projection replaces older tool observations with compact, addressable excerpts, reducing repeated input while potentially adding evidence-retrieval turns. We study this trade-off in ReVerPi, a Pi extension with archived observations and matched full/projected continuations. In an 86-run source-reading campaign with 641 model requests, the 15 completed pairs show identical success: 12/15 per arm. Twelve further boundary runs stop, with the runner suppressing the companion whenever the first arm fails to complete. Restoring all 27 boundary runs bounds projected-minus-full success between $-$9 and +1 tasks. One omitted, selector-chosen projected continuation successfully retrieves archive text yet exhausts twelve requests; its full counterpart answers in three. The eleven jointly correct pairs form a fully observed success stratum within this recorded frame: projection reduces aggregate logical tokens by 25%, while increasing the median pair's tokens by 29% and total suffix requests from 35 to 55. Separating fitting from evaluation changes the selector's apparent tie: outside its four fitting pairs, it incurs one extra failure and 8.6% more logical tokens over thirteen comparable runs. This methodological case study connects stopping rules, known bounded failures, unexecuted companions, and resource aggregation. Its findings concern the recorded campaign, rather than population noninferiority or superiority over unrestricted Pi. Evaluations should retain every intervention boundary, execute both allocated arms independently of the first arm's completion, and report completion alongside interaction and token expenditure.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates a context projection mechanism in an AI assistant by comparing "full" vs. "projected" tool contexts in a controlled campaign, finding similar task success but different token and interaction costs.
AI.motivation: Large language model agents often repeatedly resend long tool or environment histories, which is expensive. Context projection aims to compress and selectively surface prior observations, but this may require extra evidence-retrieval turns and could affect reliability. The paper wants to understand this efficiency–effectiveness trade-off and how evaluation methodology (e.g., stopping rules, unrun baselines) can bias conclusions.
AI.method: They implement context projection in ReVerPi, an extension of the Pi assistant that stores archived observations and can continue either with full history or with projected (compressed, addressable) excerpts. In a source-reading campaign, they run matched pairs of tasks: one arm uses full context, the other uses projected context. They track which tasks complete, how many model requests each arm uses, and the logical tokens consumed. They also examine “boundary runs” where evaluation was stopped early and only one arm was executed, then hypothetically restore these missing arms to bound the difference in success rates. They further separate the subset of runs used to fit a selector (choosing projection vs full) from the rest, to assess apparent performance without contamination by fitting choices.
AI.result: In 15 fully executed pairs, both full and projected arms achieve the same task success rate: 12 out of 15 each. However, the projected condition shows a 25% reduction in aggregate logical tokens across 11 jointly successful pairs, at the cost of a 29% increase in median tokens per pair and more interaction turns (suffix requests rise from 35 to 55). For twelve boundary runs where one arm was missing, completing all would bound the projected-minus-full success difference between −9 and +1 tasks, with one notable case where projection successfully retrieves archived text but needs 12 requests while full context answers in 3. When excluding the four runs used for selector fitting, the selector’s apparent tie breaks: it induces one extra failure and 8.6% more logical tokens over thirteen comparable runs.
AI.conclusion: Context projection can match the task success of full-context continuations in this campaign while changing the distribution of resource use—sometimes saving total tokens but adding turns and per-run costs. The study highlights that evaluation design (stopping early when one arm fails, not running matched companions, and mixing fitting with evaluation) can distort apparent noninferiority or efficiency. The authors argue that evaluations of such interventions should: (1) preserve all decision boundaries, (2) run both treatment arms regardless of first-arm success, and (3) report completion rates together with interaction counts and token usage. The conclusions are restricted to the recorded campaign and do not claim general superiority or noninferiority relative to unrestricted Pi in the wider population of tasks.

title: Compress What You See, Not What You Say: Anchored Context Distillation for Latent-Observation Software Engineering Agents
summary: Tool observations dominate the context of software-engineering agents, making long interaction histories costly to maintain. Existing context compression methods can discard information needed by later actions, while adapting agents to soft-token representations can compromise their original behavior. To reduce context while preserving action-critical information and agent behavior, we combine Latent Observations, Hard Actions (LOHA), a context layout that separates compressed history from text needed for exact reference, with Anchored Context Distillation (ACD), a training method that enables latent reading while constraining behavioral drift. LOHA compresses older tool observations into soft tokens while retaining the agent's own turns and the last K observations in text, providing compact access to historical information and exact access to recent content. To enable the agent to use this representation, ACD distills the base model's full-text predictions into the latent view while anchoring its behavior on plain-text inputs to the same base model. On SWE-bench Verified, K=3 reduces context per call by 43% for Qwen3-4B and 57% for SWE-Master-4B-RL, with resolve rates of 12.1% and 21.8% versus 14.5% and 27.5% for their uncompressed bases. A single-run recency sweep reaches 14.4% and 23.0% at K=8, with larger windows generally favoring task performance over compression. Under a 32K-token limit, Qwen3 with K=3 resolves 21.1% of a 199-instance subset versus 11.1% for the same adapted agent using full text. In concurrent single-GPU serving, it achieves 1.9 times that full-text agent's instance throughput.

AI.tldr: They propose a way to compress long tool-use histories for software-engineering agents while keeping performance close to an uncompressed baseline.
AI.motivation: Software-engineering agents rely heavily on long histories of tool observations (e.g., logs, traces, intermediate outputs). Keeping these in full-text form is expensive and often exceeds context limits. Existing compression either drops information that later actions may need, or forces agents to operate directly on soft-token/latent representations, which can change their behavior and hurt reliability. The authors want a method that reduces context size yet preserves the agent’s original behavior and essential information for decision-making.
AI.method: They introduce two key components. (1) Latent Observations, Hard Actions (LOHA): a context layout that keeps the agent’s own turns and the last K tool observations as plain text, while compressing older tool observations into soft tokens (latent representations). This preserves exact, readable access to recent content and compact, latent access to older history. (2) Anchored Context Distillation (ACD): a training procedure that teaches the agent to ‘read’ and use the latent observations by distilling predictions from a base model that sees the full-text context, while additionally anchoring behavior on plain-text inputs to the same base model to limit behavioral drift. Combined, LOHA+ACD allow the model to exploit compressed histories without deviating much from the original, full-text behavior.
AI.result: On the SWE-bench Verified benchmark, using K=3 (only last 3 tool observations in text) reduces per-call context size by 43% for Qwen3-4B and 57% for SWE-Master-4B-RL. Their resolve rates drop moderately to 12.1% and 21.8%, compared to 14.5% and 27.5% for uncompressed baselines, showing some performance loss but reasonable retention. A single-run sweep over K finds that at K=8, resolve rates improve to 14.4% and 23.0%, indicating that larger recent-text windows tend to favor task performance over compression. Under a 32K-token limit and on a 199-instance subset, Qwen3 with K=3 resolves 21.1% versus 11.1% for an adapted agent that uses full text, and in concurrent single-GPU serving, the K=3 configuration achieves 1.9× the instance throughput of the full-text agent.
AI.conclusion: LOHA+ACD provide an effective way to compress tool-use histories for software-engineering agents, significantly reducing context size while largely preserving task performance and original behavioral characteristics. Keeping recent observations in text and older ones in a learned latent form, plus distillation that anchors to a full-text base model, allows agents to scale to longer interactions and higher throughput under context limits. Performance trade-offs depend on the chosen recency window K, with larger K improving success rates at the cost of less compression.

title: Segment-Level Agentic Topic Modeling for Improved Data Exploration and Resource Efficiency
summary: Topic modeling is an effective technique for discovering hidden themes within documents and is widely used in text mining and data analysis across a variety of industry sectors. Recently, large language model (LLM)-based topic models have been emerged that prompt LLMs to generate topics then assign the topics to documents, producing more natural and human-readable topics than conventional topic modeling algorithms. However, the nature of topic assignment process causes certain drawbacks, such as the incapability to produce topic distributions over a document, too broad or narrow topics, and high resource consumption, which increases with the number and length of of documents being assigned topics. These issues are particularly critical for industrial applications, which require high-quality, in-depth analysis and the processing of large volumes of documents. In this context, this paper introduces a framework called SeLATM, which addresses these concerns by employing segment-level topic generation and topic refinement through agentic feedback loops. Experimental results on various datasets demonstrate that SeLATM significantly reduces the LLM resources compared to methods based on topic assignment process, while maintaining superior performance.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes SeLATM, a segment-level LLM-based topic modeling framework that uses agentic feedback loops to generate and refine topics, achieving better topic quality with much lower LLM resource usage than topic-assignment-based methods.
AI.motivation: Conventional topic models and recent LLM-based topic assignment approaches struggle in industrial settings: they produce less natural topics, cannot provide full topic distributions over documents, often yield topics that are too broad or too narrow, and consume substantial computational resources as the number and length of documents grow. There is a need for a scalable, resource-efficient LLM-based topic modeling framework that still delivers high-quality, interpretable topics and supports in-depth analysis.
AI.method: The paper introduces SeLATM, a framework that operates at the segment level rather than assigning topics to whole documents. It prompts an LLM to generate topics for smaller text segments and then uses agentic feedback loops to iteratively refine these topics. This process aims to improve topic granularity and coherence while reducing redundant or overly broad/narrow topics. The segment-level topics are then aggregated to represent documents, enabling topic distributions and scalable analysis.
AI.result: Across multiple datasets, SeLATM demonstrates that it can substantially cut LLM resource usage (e.g., fewer tokens, prompts, or model calls) compared with existing LLM-based topic assignment methods, yet still achieves equal or better performance on standard topic modeling evaluation metrics such as topic quality and interpretability.
AI.conclusion: SeLATM offers a practical, industrially suitable alternative to existing LLM-based topic modeling approaches, overcoming key limitations in topic assignment schemes. By using segment-level topic generation with agentic refinement, it yields high-quality, interpretable topics, supports topic distributions over documents, and significantly lowers LLM resource consumption on large-scale corpora.

title: Game Arena: Strategic LLM Evaluation in Competitive Environments
comment: 31 pages, 15 figures. Technical report. Project page: https://www.kaggle.com/game-arena
summary: We introduce Kaggle Game Arena, an open and ever-expanding platform to evaluate large language models (LLMs) through competitive games. Different from static benchmarks, game arena enables models to play head-to-head matchups in structured environments where the gameplay strength naturally increases as models evolve, preventing performance saturation. This technical report details the infrastructure behind Game Arena and describes the three pilot game environments: Chess, Poker, and Werewolf. These environments span perfect information, imperfect information, and multiplayer game settings, enabling a systematic study of models' strategic planning, adaptation, and robustness under uncertainty. For each game, we provide a detailed description of the environment, evaluation metrics, and results from running full competitions across models. Through robust infrastructure and large-scale ground-truth based evaluation, Game Arena ensures reproducibility, transparency and generalizability to new games and variants over time.

AI.tldr: Kaggle Game Arena is a dynamic platform to evaluate LLMs via competitive games, avoiding static-benchmark saturation.
AI.motivation: Static LLM benchmarks saturate as models improve, making it hard to differentiate capabilities. The authors want a scalable, continually challenging, and reproducible way to measure LLM strategic reasoning and robustness.
AI.method: They build an open infrastructure—Kaggle Game Arena—where LLMs play head-to-head in structured game environments. They design three pilot games (Chess, Poker, Werewolf) that cover perfect information, imperfect information, and multiplayer social deduction. For each, they define rules, interaction protocols, evaluation metrics, and run large-scale competitions between models.
AI.result: They successfully implement the platform, run full competitions across models in all three games, and obtain performance metrics that reflect models’ strategic planning, adaptation, and robustness under uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: Game Arena provides a reproducible, transparent, and extensible framework for LLM evaluation through competitive games, with potential to generalize to new games and avoid performance saturation seen in static benchmarks.

title: "AI is (not) the new...": A Diagnostic Analogy Framework for Generative AI's Cultural Impacts
summary: Generative AI is reshaping the cultural infrastructures through which knowledge is found, synthesized, and held accountable. To make sense of this shift, scholars and policymakers reach for historical analogies of technologies such as the printing press, steam power or electricity. But these comparisons are typically imprecise about which property of the technology carries the comparison, and imprecise analogies produce imprecise governance by designing interventions against the wrong property of the system. This paper offers a diagnostic framework for analyzing how generative AI can transform epistemic and cultural practice. This paper offers a diagnostic framework for analyzing how generative AI can transform epistemic and cultural practice. We decompose each intervention into three coordinates: the epistemic site at which a technology acts, the governing logic by which it organizes its object, and the technical mechanism through which the logic is instantiated. This framework allows us to distinguish between structural cultural consequences, which follow from the mechanism itself, from contingent ones, which remain open to design and institutional choice. Applying the framework to information discovery and knowledge synthesis, we show how the shift from indexicality to inference and from editorial authority to statistical consensus produces specific, traceable cultural effects and reveals governance levers that gestalt analogy obscures.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a framework to precisely compare generative AI with past technologies in terms of how they change knowledge practices and culture, in order to guide better governance and design.
AI.motivation: Existing debates about generative AI rely on loose historical analogies (e.g., printing press, electricity) that do not specify which aspects of the technologies are being compared. Such vagueness leads to misguided regulatory and institutional responses because they target the wrong properties of the systems. There is a need for a clearer, more diagnostic way to understand how generative AI actually transforms epistemic and cultural practices, particularly around information discovery and knowledge synthesis.
AI.method: The authors construct a conceptual/diagnostic framework. They decompose any technological intervention into three dimensions: (1) the epistemic site where the technology operates (e.g., discovery, synthesis, validation), (2) the governing logic it uses to organize its objects (e.g., indexicality vs. inference, editorial authority vs. statistical consensus), and (3) the technical mechanism that instantiates this logic. They then apply this framework to generative AI in the domains of information discovery and knowledge synthesis to analyze its cultural and epistemic impacts.
AI.result: Using this three-coordinate framework, the authors differentiate structural cultural consequences of generative AI (those stemming directly from its mechanisms and governing logic) from contingent consequences that can be shaped by design and institutions. They show that generative AI marks a move from index-based retrieval to inferential generation, and from reliance on human editorial judgment to statistical aggregation of consensus, each with traceable cultural and epistemic effects. The framework surfaces specific governance levers that are missed when AI is discussed via broad, gestalt analogies to past technologies.
AI.conclusion: The framework clarifies how generative AI reshapes knowledge infrastructures and cultural practices by specifying where it acts, how it governs information, and through what technical means. This precision enables more targeted governance and design interventions, distinguishing between what is structurally baked into the technology and what remains open to institutional choice. As a result, policymakers and scholars can move beyond vague historical analogies toward a more rigorous understanding of generative AI’s epistemic and cultural implications.

title: UQ-LOB: Uncertainty-Aware Limit Order Book Mid-Price Forecasting
summary: Forecasting short-horizon mid-price movements from limit order book (LOB) data is central to algorithmic trading, yet most deep LOB forecasters are point predictors: they output a direction or a displacement, but never indicate which of their forecasts can be trusted. We introduce UQ-LOB, a lightweight, encoder-agnostic uncertainty quantification module that attaches to any pretrained LOB encoder and, in the spirit of attentive neural processes, conditions each forecast on a context set of recently completed windows whose outcomes are already realised. The UQ-regression variant outputs a calibrated Gaussian over the future tick displacement, while the UQ-classification variant outputs a categorical distribution over down/up/stationary. Both expose a scalar confidence (predicted signal-to-noise ratio or class probability) that supports selective prediction. On 5.2 billion LOB events across seven cryptocurrency assets and horizons of 5, 10 and 15 seconds, UQ-regression attains near-nominal 68% interval coverage, and restricting to the most confident 10% of predictions raises directional macro F1 by 0.11-0.15 for UQ-regression and 0.05-0.11 for UQ-classification, at every horizon. On large, economically meaningful moves, the tightest confidence tier reaches a directional F1 of 0.88 (down) and 0.83 (up) at the 5-second horizon.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes UQ-LOB, an uncertainty-aware forecasting module for limit order book mid-price movements that attaches to any pretrained encoder and provides calibrated probabilistic predictions and confidence scores, improving performance especially when focusing on the most confident forecasts.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning models for limit order book data usually produce point predictions about future price movements (direction or magnitude) without indicating how reliable each prediction is. In algorithmic trading, knowing when to trust a forecast is crucial for risk management, position sizing, and selective execution. There is a need for a lightweight, general approach to add uncertainty estimates and confidence-based selection to existing LOB forecasters.
AI.method: The authors design UQ-LOB, a small, encoder-agnostic module that can be attached to any pretrained LOB encoder. Inspired by attentive neural processes, UQ-LOB conditions predictions on a context set comprising recently completed windows whose true outcomes are already known. Two variants are proposed: (1) UQ-regression, which outputs a Gaussian distribution over future tick displacement and a signal-to-noise ratio as a confidence measure, and (2) UQ-classification, which produces a categorical distribution over down/up/stationary movements and uses class probabilities as confidence. Both variants enable selective prediction by allowing the user to focus on high-confidence cases. The models are trained and evaluated on large-scale LOB data from multiple cryptocurrency assets and multiple short forecasting horizons.
AI.result: On a dataset of 5.2 billion LOB events across seven cryptocurrency assets and forecast horizons of 5, 10, and 15 seconds, UQ-regression achieves close-to-nominal 68% coverage for its predictive intervals, indicating good calibration. When restricting evaluation to the top 10% most confident predictions (according to the module’s confidence scores), directional macro F1 scores improve substantially: by 0.11–0.15 for UQ-regression and 0.05–0.11 for UQ-classification across all horizons. For large and economically significant price movements, the most confident predictions reach high directional F1 scores, up to 0.88 for down moves and 0.83 for up moves at the 5-second horizon.
AI.conclusion: UQ-LOB effectively augments existing LOB forecasting models with calibrated uncertainty estimates and actionable confidence scores, enabling selective prediction that significantly boosts accuracy on high-confidence cases. The approach is lightweight, encoder-agnostic, and scales to billions of events, making it practical for real-world algorithmic trading. Its strong performance on large price moves suggests particular value for trading strategies that focus on impactful events and require robust risk-aware decision making.

title: Prompt Minimization: Reducing Input Redundancy Without Sacrificing Output Fidelity
summary: Despite the growing capabilities of large language models (LLMs), prompt design remains largely heuristic and ad hoc. This project will explore $\textit{prompt minimization}$, the process of reducing prompts to their smallest, most information-dense form while preserving output fidelity. Practically, shorter prompts reduce computational overhead and inference latency, especially when large contexts, such as entire documents or codebases, are included unnecessarily. Further, longer prompts can damage LLM reasoning and accuracy. Theoretically, the existence of multiple prompts yielding equivalent outputs suggests a high degree of redundancy in the input space, raising fundamental questions about what information is essential to elicit specific model behaviors. We propose three variant frameworks to identify and evaluate minimal prompts and demonstrate that minimal prompts often produce outputs comparable to those of their longer counterparts. These findings suggest new directions for efficient prompt engineering and deepen our understanding of input compression in LLMs.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how to shorten prompts for large language models while keeping answer quality the same.
AI.motivation: Prompt design for LLMs is currently informal and inefficient; long prompts increase cost and latency and can even hurt reasoning. Since different prompts can give the same outputs, there is redundancy, and it is unclear which parts of the input are truly necessary to elicit a behavior.
AI.method: The authors define and study “prompt minimization,” proposing three frameworks for finding and evaluating minimal prompts that still preserve output fidelity. They systematically reduce prompts and test whether model outputs remain equivalent or comparable to those from longer prompts.
AI.result: They find that many prompts can be substantially shortened without degrading the quality of the LLM’s outputs. Minimal prompts identified by their frameworks often achieve performance similar to that obtained with original, longer prompts.
AI.conclusion: Prompt minimization is feasible and useful: it can reduce computational cost, maintain or even improve reasoning, and reveals redundancy in LLM input space. This opens new directions for more efficient prompt engineering and for understanding input compression and essential information for LLM behavior.

title: A Flow Matching Framework for Neural Representational Dissimilarity
summary: Neural representational dissimilarity quantifies differences between neural response distributions, and is essential for comparing neural codes across stimuli, brain areas, tasks, and models. Commonly used distance metrics involve different assumptions and are estimated with separate methods. Here, we show that a variety of distance metrics can be unified under a flow matching framework developed in deep generative models. That is, these distances arise as Jeffreys divergences under different velocity constraints. We find that flow matching has advantages for estimating distances involving complicated distributions and continuous variables. Furthermore, this framework enables the design of new distance metrics in a principled way. Together, flow matching provides a unified approach for understanding, estimating, and designing neural representational dissimilarity metrics.
