AI.tldr: They unify many neural representational distance metrics using a flow matching framework from generative modeling, showing these metrics are Jeffreys divergences under different velocity constraints, which helps estimate and design dissimilarity measures for complex neural data.
AI.motivation: Neuroscientists need reliable ways to quantify how different neural responses are across stimuli, brain areas, tasks, and models. Existing representational dissimilarity measures (e.g., various distance/divergence metrics) rely on heterogeneous assumptions and estimation methods, making them hard to compare, extend, or apply to complex, continuous neural response distributions. A principled, unified framework is missing.
AI.method: They reinterpret commonly used neural representational distance metrics within the mathematical framework of flow matching from deep generative models. Concretely, they show that many distances can be written as Jeffreys divergences that arise from probability flows constrained by different velocity fields. They then use flow matching techniques to estimate these distances for complex and continuous neural response distributions and to construct new metrics by specifying new velocity constraints.
AI.result: They demonstrate that diverse representational dissimilarity metrics can all be seen as special cases of Jeffreys divergences within a flow matching formulation. Using this view, they show practical advantages in estimating distances for complicated or continuous neural response distributions compared with standard estimators. They also illustrate how new, tailored distance metrics can be derived systematically by designing appropriate flow/velocity constraints.
AI.conclusion: Flow matching offers a unified theoretical and computational framework for neural representational dissimilarity. It connects multiple existing distance metrics via Jeffreys divergences, improves estimation for complex neural data, and provides principled tools to design new dissimilarity measures. This unification can streamline comparisons of neural codes and foster more flexible, well-founded metrics in systems and computational neuroscience.

title: Multi-agent Scaling Across Disjunctive and Compensatory Tasks
summary: Multi-agent LLM systems are often expected to improve as team size increases, yet the scaling behavior may depend on task structure. Our central contribution is to introduce Steiner's taxonomy of group tasks as a framework for analyzing multi-agent LLM scaling and focusing the analysis on disjunctive and compensatory tasks. We model independently sampled agents as conditionally independent given the item, which yields their large-team limits: plurality voting converges to the model's modal answer, and averaging converges to the model's item-level bias. Across selected representative benchmarks, 13 open-weight models, and teams of up to 30 agents, we find qualitatively different scaling behavior. On disjunctive tasks, the probability that at least one agent is correct grows by 5-20 points with team size, but plurality voting over agents that answer directly realises almost none of this potential, as the model predicts to within 0.5 points on average. Multi-round revision raises accuracy considerably, yet the gain is nearly the same with one peer as with 29. In contrast, scaling provides little benefit on Fermi estimation, despite its natural suitability for aggregation: item-level biases shared across the samples of a model account for about 87% of the squared error, so averaging reduces error by only about 6%. Combining model families helps on Fermi estimation but does not surpass the strongest member on disjunctive tasks. These results show that task structure, together with the mechanism combining member outputs, is a fundamental determinant of team scaling.

AI.tldr: The paper studies how performance of multi-agent LLM teams scales with team size, showing that gains depend strongly on task type and aggregation method, and are often much smaller than naive intuition suggests.
AI.motivation: Many people expect that using more LLM agents in a team will automatically improve performance, but empirical behavior has been mixed and poorly understood. The authors aim to provide a principled framework to reason about when and why adding more LLM agents helps or fails, using classic group task theory (Steiner's taxonomy) to structure this analysis.
AI.method: The authors map multi-agent LLM use cases onto Steiner’s taxonomy, focusing on disjunctive tasks (success if at least one agent is correct) and compensatory tasks (where outputs can be averaged). They model multiple agents as independent samples from the same base model, conditionally independent given the item. Under this model, they derive large-team limits for two aggregation strategies: plurality voting and averaging. They then empirically evaluate scaling behavior on representative benchmarks using 13 open-weight models and teams up to 30 agents, with different aggregation mechanisms including direct-answer voting, multi-round revision, averaging for Fermi-estimation, and mixing model families.
AI.result: For disjunctive tasks, the theoretical probability that at least one agent is correct increases by 5–20 percentage points as the team grows, but naive plurality voting over direct answers captures almost none of this potential; performance closely matches the single-model prediction within 0.5 points. Multi-round peer-based revision significantly increases accuracy, but nearly all of the benefit is already obtained with just one peer, and adding up to 29 more agents yields little further improvement. For compensatory Fermi-estimation tasks, expanding team size brings only modest gains: around 87% of squared error arises from shared item-level bias across samples from a model, so averaging reduces error by only about 6%. Combining different model families helps for Fermi estimation by reducing shared bias, but this ensemble does not outperform the strongest individual model on disjunctive tasks.
AI.conclusion: The effectiveness of scaling up multi-agent LLM teams is not universal; it is tightly constrained by task structure and the aggregation mechanism. For disjunctive tasks, simple voting among many similar agents fails to exploit the potential benefit of having at least one correct agent, and more elaborate multi-round collaboration shows strong diminishing returns beyond very small teams. For compensatory tasks like Fermi estimation, shared biases dominate error, so averaging many same-family agents yields little improvement; only diversity across model families helps somewhat. Overall, task type and combination strategy are fundamental determinants of whether larger LLM teams will provide meaningful gains, challenging the assumption that “more agents is always better.”

title: DeepEdu-v1: Efficient and Scalable Agentic LLMs for Vietnamese Education
summary: AI tutoring could markedly improve learning outcomes for students in developing regions such as Vietnam, yet the two obvious paths both fall short. Cloud assistants such as ChatGPT route sensitive student data to foreign servers---violating data-sovereignty laws such as Vietnam's Decree 53---and, pre-trained on Western-centric corpora, are not organized around the national textbook curriculum, so their knowledge of local content is unsystematic and frequently hallucinated. Self-hosting an open model keeps data on-premise but hits a two-fold wall: post-training quantization (AWQ, GPTQ) tames the static weight footprint, yet the dynamic KV cache and prefill latency of long tutoring contexts still cause out-of-memory failures and slow responses on consumer GPUs, while the model keeps hallucinating on region-specific material. We present DeepEdu-v1, an AI-tutoring system for Vietnamese education built on SCALE (Self-improving Context-Aware Learning Engine), a framework with two innovations. First, a long-context inference engine amortizes token selection from per-sub-chunk to per-cluster granularity; on long-context retrieval it issues x7.7 fewer retrieval calls than a state-of-the-art selective-attention baseline, cutting prefill latency (TTFT) by roughly 35% while matching or improving task accuracy. Second, a self-improving agentic layer continuously curates a verified playbook from past interactions instead of fine-tuning, a design intended to progressively reduce reliance on dominant-language priors as trustworthy local knowledge accumulates. In its deployed configuration, DeepEdu achieves a nearly x2 TTFT speedup over standard vLLM serving and lifts agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5% on complex tasks, with the strongest per-track gains across financial-reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks.

AI.tldr: DeepEdu-v1 introduces SCALE, a context-efficient and self-improving AI tutoring system tailored to Vietnamese education, achieving faster inference and higher agentic accuracy without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: Existing AI tutoring paths for regions like Vietnam are problematic: cloud-based assistants violate data-sovereignty regulations and lack alignment with national curricula, while self-hosted open models struggle with GPU memory/latency and hallucinate on local content. There is a need for an efficient, locally deployable, and curriculum-grounded tutoring system that respects legal constraints and improves over time on region-specific knowledge.
AI.method: The authors build DeepEdu-v1 on SCALE, which has two main components: (1) a long-context inference engine that amortizes token selection by operating at per-cluster rather than per-sub-chunk granularity, sharply reducing retrieval calls and prefill latency compared with selective-attention baselines; and (2) a self-improving agentic layer that incrementally constructs a verified playbook from prior interactions instead of relying on traditional fine-tuning, thereby shifting the model away from dominant-language priors towards trustworthy local knowledge.
AI.result: On long-context retrieval tasks, the new inference engine issues about 7.7x fewer retrieval calls than a state-of-the-art selective-attention baseline and reduces time-to-first-token by roughly 35% while maintaining or improving task accuracy. In its deployed setup, DeepEdu nearly doubles TTFT performance compared with standard vLLM serving and increases agentic accuracy from 70.0% to 79.5% on complex tasks, with particularly strong improvements on financial-reasoning and interactive-agent benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: SCALE-powered DeepEdu-v1 demonstrates that a locally deployable AI-tutoring system can both meet data-sovereignty constraints and deliver efficient, accurate, and progressively improving support for a national curriculum. Its cluster-based long-context inference reduces latency and resource usage, and its self-improving agentic layer provides a practical alternative to fine-tuning for accumulating reliable, region-specific educational knowledge.
